name: Streaming-response caching via chunk accumulation + ordered replay (Bifrost)
mechanism: Every stream chunk arriving in PostLLMHook is appended to a per-request sync.Map-backed StreamAccumulator (stream.go:45-79). On the final chunk, processAccumulatedStream() sort.SliceStable's the chunks by (Index, ChunkIndex) — necessary because chunks are NOT guaranteed to arrive in order — then json.Marshal's each and stores the ordered array as metadata['stream_chunks'] in one cache write (stream.go:81-133). A background reaper (streamAccumulatorMaxAge=5min) drops abandoned accumulators from client disconnects or mid-stream provider errors so they don't leak memory.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: medium-high — the sort-by-chunk-index + abandoned-stream reaping + the explicit 'don't double-write a cache-hit replay's own chunks back into the store' guard (main.go:572-580, citing a real Weaviate 422 'id already exists' bug they hit and fixed) show this took real iteration to get right.
trap: Race explicitly documented and guarded against in code comments: on a cache-hit replay of a stream, PostLLMHook runs once per replayed chunk and must NOT re-write those replayed chunks as if they were a fresh miss (state.ShortCircuited guard, main.go:572-580) or you get a duplicate-key write error. Also: caching a stream requires holding EVERY chunk in memory until the final one arrives — a client that disconnects mid-stream just leaves that generation uncached (never flushed) rather than partially cached.

name: Bucket-of-N cached responses with random selection on hit (Helicone)
mechanism: kvKeyFromRequest() hashes (cacheSeed + url + raw-body-with-ignored-keys-stripped + JSON.stringify(relevant headers, including Authorization) + a positional freeIndex) with a plain string concatenation — no JSON canonicalization, so key order in headers/body matters. getMaxCachedResponses() does bucketSize parallel KV.get() calls (one per freeIndex slot) via Promise.all to find which slots are filled; getCachedResponse() picks Math.floor(Math.random() * requestCaches.length) among the filled slots. A fill only happens once all bucketSize slots are populated (freeIndexes.length===0); until then every request is a guaranteed miss and adds one more sample to the bucket.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: low to build, but bucketSize KV round-trips per request lookup (all awaited in parallel) is real infra cost that scales with bucket size — worth benchmarking before assuming this is 'free'.
trap: This is the single most direct, concrete acknowledgment in the whole ecosystem of the exact Tier-B temperature caveat in your brief — but it is NOT sold as such in Helicone's docs, it's just how the cache backend happens to be built. If you cite this as prior art you should be precise: it does not draw a fresh sample, it uniformly resamples from up to 20 historical draws, which converges to the true distribution only in the limit of large bucketSize and stationary model behavior (a model update between draws silently poisons the bucket with stale-distribution samples).

name: Streaming-response caching via chunk-array storage + synthetic ReadableStream replay (Helicone)
mechanism: trySaveToCache() stores responseBody: string[] (the raw chunk texts) directly in the KV value alongside headers/latency. getCachedResponse() reconstructs a real ReadableStream that synchronously enqueues each stored chunk in original order via a recursive pushChunk(), so downstream SSE parsing code sees an indistinguishable stream.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: low — much simpler than Bifrost's implementation (no cross-chunk ordering problem because the KV write happens once, after the whole stream has already been assembled server-side by the proxy).
trap: The replayed stream has none of the original inter-chunk timing — all chunks are enqueued back-to-back with no delay, so client-side code that infers anything from streaming cadence (e.g. a 'typing speed' UI) will behave differently on a cache hit vs. a live call. That is a Tier-A-violating side channel if your product's promise is 'the output is provably unaffected' — worth explicit note if you replicate this.

name: kwargs-order-dependent string-concat cache key (LiteLLM exact cache)
mechanism: Cache.get_cache_key() (litellm/caching/caching.py:328-378) iterates `for param in kwargs:` (Python dict = insertion-order-preserving, NOT alphabetically sorted) and does `cache_key += f"{param}: {param_value}"` — i.e. it is a raw string concatenation over dict iteration order, not a canonical/sorted serialization. The result is SHA-256 hashed via hashlib (_get_hashed_cache_key, line 458-474) and optionally namespaced. There is a 'preset_cache_key' fast-path (lines 341-344, 431-455) that memoizes the computed key onto litellm_params so repeated internal calls in one request lifecycle don't recompute it — that part is a legitimate Tier-A optimization (pure compute reuse, same key either way).
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: low to reproduce, but the lack of canonicalization (contrast with Bifrost's MarshalDeeplySorted, explicitly built because Go map iteration order is randomized) is a design gap unless kwargs order is provably deterministic everywhere it's constructed.
trap: No sort/canonicalization step at all, unlike every other exact-cache implementation reviewed (Cloudflare hashes the raw wire body — deterministic because it's the literal JSON string, not a reconstructed dict; Portkey similarly hashes JSON.stringify(requestBody), the wire body; Bifrost explicitly built MarshalDeeplySorted BECAUSE it doesn't trust map order). LiteLLM is the one reviewed implementation building its hash input from a re-serialized kwargs dict without sorting, which is the riskiest pattern of the group even though a concrete collision was not proven.
sources: github.com/BerriAI/litellm litellm/caching/caching.py (lines 328-378, 457-474) — fetched via gh api 2026-08-10

name: Self-healing embedding/scalar-store desync detector (GPTCache cache_health_check)
mechanism: adapter.py's cache_health_check() compares the embedding stored in the vector index against the embedding retrievable from the scalar/object store for the same entry id; on mismatch it forces the similarity score to -inf (invalidating that candidate for this lookup) and 'self-heals' by overwriting the vector store's embedding with the scalar store's copy.
savings: N/A — this is a data-integrity guard, not a cost technique
effort: low
trap: This exists because two independently-updatable stores (vector index + scalar/metadata store) can silently desync — a real operational hazard for anyone building a similar dual-store semantic cache, not unique to GPTCache.

name: Exact SHA-256 hash of (provider, endpoint, model, auth header, full request body) — no canonicalization needed, no semantic cache
mechanism: Cloudflare AI Gateway hashes provider + endpoint + model + the provider auth bearer token + the complete raw request body with SHA-256 to form the cache key. Because it hashes the literal wire body (not a reconstructed/reserialized object), it is inherently canonical — there's no reserialization step to introduce order-sensitivity, unlike LiteLLM's kwargs-reconstruction approach.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — Cloudflare's own docs give no hit-rate or dollar figures.
effort: low
trap: Because the AUTH HEADER is part of the key, two different API keys/customers calling with byte-identical prompts get separate cache entries — no accidental cross-tenant leakage, but also no cross-tenant savings (a real design tradeoff worth being explicit about if you build a multi-tenant version). Also: this doc explicitly states cache applies only to text and image responses, not other media types.
sources: developers.cloudflare.com/ai-gateway/features/caching/ — fetched via WebFetch 2026-08-10 (provider's own reference docs)

name: No request coalescing — Cloudflare's own docs admit concurrent duplicate requests are NOT deduplicated
mechanism: N/A. Direct quote from Cloudflare's own docs: 'If two identical requests are sent simultaneously, the first request may not cache in time for the second request to use it.' No lock, no promise-sharing, no request-in-flight registry — each concurrent duplicate independently misses and independently calls the upstream provider.
savings: N/A
effort: N/A
trap: This is the single biggest finding relevant to the 'double-bill on retry / concurrent duplicate' question: I read the caching source of five different gateways (LiteLLM's caching.py/dual_cache.py, Portkey's memoryCache middleware, Helicone's cacheFunctions.ts, Bifrost's semanticcache plugin) looking specifically for a mutex/SETNX/singleflight/promise-registry pattern guarding concurrent identical requests, and found NONE in any of them. Every one is a pure lookaside cache: check → (miss) → call upstream → write. N concurrent identical requests during the fill window = N full-price upstream calls, in every reviewed implementation. Cloudflare is simply the only one that says so in writing. If your product implements true single-flight/dogpile prevention, that is a genuinely uncommon feature in this space, not an already-solved problem — worth re-verifying against each repo's latest commits before building a pitch on it, since this is exactly the kind of claim that ages badly.

github.com/portkey-ai/gateway src/middlewares/cache/index.ts (plain JS object, no lock)

name: Provider-native prompt-cache passthrough via sticky-routing key (OpenRouter)
mechanism: Per OpenRouter's docs: absent an explicit session_id (request field or x-session-id header, up to 256 chars) or an OpenAI-style prompt_cache_key field, OpenRouter derives a sticky-routing key by hashing the first system/developer message plus the first non-system message of the request, and uses that to keep routing subsequent calls in the same logical session to the same provider endpoint — maximizing the odds that provider-side caching (Anthropic prompt caching, OpenAI's automatic prefix cache) actually hits.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: low conceptually (a routing hint), but only as good as the reliability of the load balancer actually honoring stickiness under provider failover.
trap: This ONLY works for the FIRST two messages of a conversation, not the full accumulated context — a long multi-turn conversation could still fail to route to the same provider mid-conversation if the routing key is only derived once from the opening messages and the underlying load balancer doesn't persist stickiness across the whole session lifetime reliably. Session-stickiness TTL/durability was not stated in the docs reached — flagged as an open question.

name: Exact hash of JSON.stringify(body)+url, streaming excluded entirely (Portkey OSS gateway 'simple' cache)
mechanism: getCacheKey() concatenates JSON.stringify(requestBody) + '-' + url and SHA-256's it via the WebCrypto subtle API (runs on Cloudflare Workers). putInCache() explicitly bails with a comment 'Does not support caching of streams' when requestBody.stream is truthy. The cache store itself is a plain in-process JS object (const inMemoryCache: any = {}) — the OSS gateway's built-in cache is a single-worker-instance memory cache, not a distributed store; it will not share hits across Worker isolates/instances at all in a real Cloudflare deployment.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: low
trap: Two traps: (1) JSON.stringify on a JS object is insertion-order-dependent for keys the same way Python dict iteration is — no canonicalization, same class of risk as LiteLLM's kwargs concat; (2) the in-memory cache is process-local. In a real multi-instance Workers deployment, most requests will simply never see a hit from another isolate — this OSS 'simple' cache is effectively a demo/dev-mode cache. The CACHE_STATUS enum literally has SEMANTIC_HIT/SEMANTIC_MISS constants defined but there is NO semantic-cache implementation code anywhere in the repo (confirmed via GitHub code search for 'semantic' across portkey-ai/gateway — zero source-code hits, only docs/notebooks) — semantic caching is a Portkey Cloud (closed-source) feature, not in the OSS gateway.

name: litellm cache_control_injection_points (proxy-layer auto cache_control injection)
mechanism: LiteLLM's completion params accept cache_control_injection_points: a list of {location: 'message'|'tool_config', role or index}. litellm/integrations/anthropic_cache_control_hook.py resolves targets by role (all messages of that role) or by index (supports negative indices), skips messages that already carry client-set cache_control (won't overwrite an existing TTL), reserves one of the 4 breakpoint slots for tool_config if present, stops injecting once the 4-breakpoint ceiling is hit (with a warning), and for native /v1/messages requests processes system-prompt injection before message injection to respect provider ordering. Purely a transport-layer rewrite of the outgoing request body — model receives the same bytes it would if you'd hand-added cache_control yourself.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED (no benchmark given in docs; savings equal whatever manual cache_control placement would yield)
effort: low — one config block (cache_control_injection_points: [...]) per model in LiteLLM config/router, no app code change
trap: Widely re-implemented on top of by other frameworks (dspy, Strix, SurfSense, PR-Agent, paper-qa, beeai-framework, Kiln-AI, ZhuLinsen daily_stock_analysis all wrap it per code search) — if LiteLLM silently drops an injection point past the 4-breakpoint cap, every one of those downstream tools inherits the miss with only a log-level warning, not an error.
