name: langchain_anthropic AnthropicPromptCachingMiddleware
mechanism: Tags the last content block of the system message and the last tool definition with cache_control:{type:'ephemeral', ttl:'5m' default}, so system+tools cache together across turns. min_messages_to_cache=0 by default (caches immediately). Ships as opt-in middleware in create_agent.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: low — add one middleware entry
trap: CONFIRMED bug (langchain/langchain#33709): if ModelFallbackMiddleware kicks in after the Anthropic call fails, the same message objects — still carrying cache_control — get forwarded to the fallback provider (e.g. OpenAI), which rejects the unknown kwarg with a TypeError. unsupported_model_behavior='ignore' only suppresses the warning, it does not strip the field. Net effect: enabling caching for resilience can take down your fallback path entirely.

name: msglm mk_msg_anthropic/mk_msgs_anthropic cache= / ttl= / cache_last_ckpt_only=
mechanism: Python helper library (AnswerDotAI/msglm). cache=True converts string content to [{type:text,...}] and appends cache_control to the final content element; ttl= embeds {ttl: ...} unvalidated; cache_last_ckpt_only=True strips cache_control from all prior messages via _remove_cache_ckpts() before applying it only to the newest message, so you don't silently exceed the 4-breakpoint cap as history grows.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: low — library call at message-construction time
trap: ttl value is embedded without validation — passing a non-Anthropic-accepted string produces a 400 only at request time, not at call time.

name: Builder-declared stable-prefix registry (split scaffold from volatile tail at construction time)
mechanism: Process-local registry (seen verbatim across NousResearch/hermes-agent, zed-wong/hermesbot, plm66/hermes-delegate, xRetr00/Marvi — apparently a shared agent-framework fork lineage). Instead of re-parsing a fixed-format string at request time to find where static scaffold ends and volatile tail (timestamps, ticket payload, run context) begins, the builder that concatenates the two calls register_stable_prefix(prefix) at construction time — the one place that provably knows the exact byte boundary. find_stable_prefix(content) then returns the longest registered prefix that is a *proper* prefix of the current message, letting the cache planner split it into a cached block + a fresh volatile block instead of caching (or missing on) the whole concatenated string. LRU-evicted at 32 entries / 4MB total chars. This is the documented anthropics/skills.md pattern ('mark end of shared portion only, not the entire prompt') productionized for webhook/cron/skill-triggered agent turns where the volatile tail changes every invocation.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED (code comments describe it as fixing 'per-invocation full rewrite' for webhook/cron workloads specifically, no dollar figure)
effort: medium — requires the caller to register the exact static prefix bytes at construction time, and requires trusting the registry across process restarts is NOT preserved by design (falls back to whole-message caching on miss)
trap: Regex/marker-string heuristics for finding the boundary are explicitly rejected in the code comments because marker text can legitimately appear inside skill bodies or quoted event payloads (e.g. a helpdesk ticket transcript), silently shrinking the cached prefix or worse, absorbing volatile bytes into the 'stable' cache and reintroducing per-invocation misses. I did not independently verify that splitting one string into two adjacent 'text' content blocks in the Anthropic Messages API tokenizes byte-identically to a single block — I infer it does from the officially documented breakpoint-placement pattern, but did not run the API to confirm no separator token is inserted between array elements.

name: prompt-cache-key / prompt-cache-key-rs — canonical hash of cacheable scope for worker routing
mechanism: Canonicalizes {model, system blocks up to the last cache_control breakpoint, tools} into stable JSON, SHA-256 hashes it, prefixes with model name (anthropic-cache:<model>:sha256:<hash>). Content after the last breakpoint is deliberately excluded from the hash since it's outside Anthropic's cached scope. Workers/routers use the identical local hash to route related requests to whichever process/instance is likely to already hold a warm server-side cache, without a network round-trip.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: low — ~100 LOC, zero deps per author's own description
trap: Only as good as your load balancer actually honoring the hash for routing decisions — the key computation itself does nothing without a sticky-routing layer wired to consume it.

name: prompt-cache-warmer / prompt-cache-warmer-rs — synthetic priming request
mechanism: Fires a request through the same static prefix (with a cache_control breakpoint) ahead of real user traffic, so the 5m/1h TTL clock is already running when the first real request arrives, converting what would be the first request's cache-write into a cache-read. Pairs with cachebench for hit-rate verification.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: low-medium — requires a scheduler to re-fire the warmer inside the TTL window (every <5min for ephemeral default, <1h for the 1h beta)
trap: Warming costs a full cache-write (1.25x or 2x) every TTL interval even during idle periods with zero real traffic — can net-negative on low-QPS services if the warm interval is shorter than real request cadence.

name: cachebench / cachebench-rs — per-call hit-ratio + cost + regression-alert instrumentation
mechanism: Reads cache_read_input_tokens / cache_creation_input_tokens (and OpenAI/Bedrock equivalents) off each response, computes hit ratio and cost saved via (cache_read*read_rate) - (cache_creation*write_rate) + (input*input_rate) using configurable per-provider pricing. Fires alerts (stderr or on_miss_alert callback) when hit ratio for a request with a known-cacheable prefix drops below a configurable threshold (default 60%). CachePolicy.miss_aware() retries once after a delay to work around what the author calls an 'eventual-consistency window' where a cache hit silently misses on the immediately-following request.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED (observation tool, not itself a savings lever)
effort: low — wraps existing API calls
trap: The claimed 'eventual-consistency window' behind miss_aware() retry logic is asserted by the tool author without citing an Anthropic-side SLA or incident report — I could not independently verify server-side cache-write propagation delay as a documented phenomenon; treat that specific claim as unsourced pending confirmation.

name: bedrockcache — 6-layer breakpoint/threshold audit across Bedrock abstraction stacks
mechanism: Statically validates cache directive placement and translation across 6 distinct call paths to Claude-on-Bedrock: raw Converse API cachePoint blocks, InvokeModel+Anthropic-body cache_control (+required beta headers for older models), boto3 AnthropicBedrock, LiteLLM completion(), Strands BedrockModel cache_points, and pydantic-ai's Bedrock extra_body passthrough — checking the ≥1024-token segment minimum and the 4-breakpoint cap at each layer.
providers: Anthropic via AWS Bedrock, via LiteLLM/Strands/pydantic-ai wrappers
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: medium — one-off audit run per deployment
trap: Directly evidences the cline#12913 dialect-mismatch class of bug: any layer that emits Anthropic-format cache_control instead of Bedrock Converse-format cachePoint silently no-ops rather than erroring.

name: prompt-pillar — find_stable_prefix() diagnostic across N historical message-list runs
mechanism: Given multiple past agent-run message lists, walks them in lockstep comparing messages for semantic equality regardless of dict key ordering, returning the longest common prefix, the index/summary of first divergence, and an estimated-cacheable-token count. 'If the prefix is smaller than you expected, something in your agent is mutating the prompt prefix between calls' — used to locate the exact message where an app is accidentally breaking its own cache.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: low — feed it captured request logs offline
trap: None documented; purely diagnostic, doesn't touch live traffic.

name: prompt-cache-doctor — byte-level diff detector for silent invalidators
mechanism: Performs exact byte-level diffs between consecutive API calls to surface exactly what changed in the prefix, then correlates against cache-miss events. Also runs a breakpoint-placement audit checking whether existing cache_control markers actually maximize cached-token coverage. Author-documented scope: reliably detects system-prompt and tool-ordering misses as of v0.1; message-level and RAG document-set drift detection are listed as unimplemented roadmap items, not shipped detections.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: low
trap: v0.1 explicitly does not detect message-level or RAG-retrieval-drift causes of misses despite the tool's tagline promising general 'cache hit rate diagnosis' — a user relying on a clean report from this tool alone would miss an entire class of causes.

name: cache-audit — 6-rule static audit (ordering, injection, tool/model stability, dynamic-content size, fork safety)
mechanism: Claude Code skill scoring a setup against 6 rules: (1) no dynamic data (timestamps, git status) in the system prompt prefix, (2) system-prompt edits must go through <system-reminder> tags rather than mid-session prefix mutation, (3) no adding/removing tools mid-conversation, (4) no model switching within a thread, (5) cap volume of injected dynamic content per session, (6) compaction/subagent forks must share the parent's prefix ('fork safety').
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: low
trap: README attributes these as '6 rules from Anthropic's engineering team' but I could not find that exact 6-rule enumeration in Anthropic's own primary docs (the anthropics/skills prompt-caching.md I fetched covers overlapping ground under different framing/count) — treat the 'official Anthropic engineering team' attribution itself as an unverified/likely-repackaged claim, even though the underlying substance (rules 1, 3, 4, 6) is independently corroborated by the primary doc and by cache-refund/cnighswonger findings below.

name: cache-refund — gap-classification of recoverable vs unrecoverable cache misses from transcripts
mechanism: Parses Claude Code transcripts, buckets inter-turn gaps by cause: TTL expiry (300-3600s gap = 'recoverable' leak, i.e. would have hit under 1h TTL), cold start (session init, unfixable), model switch mid-session (fixable), server-side compaction rewrite (partially fixable), cross-session isolation (uncontrollable). Also reads usage.cache_creation.ephemeral_{5m,1h}_input_tokens directly to determine which TTL regime actually shipped on a given request, independent of what was requested.
savings: Recommends switching to 1h TTL 'when R/C exceeds 39.47% threshold' — this specific number is the tool's own derived break-even, not independently audited by me
effort: low — offline analysis of existing transcript logs
trap: The 39.47% break-even threshold is presented without a shown derivation in the README excerpt I fetched — plausible given documented 1.25x/2x write multipliers and 0.1x read rate, but I did not re-derive it myself; flag as inferred-but-unverified.

name: Deterministic serialization discipline (sort_keys=True, sorted tool lists, no set iteration in prefix)
mechanism: Anthropic's own skill doc names non-deterministic JSON serialization, dict/set iteration order, and unsorted tool lists as 'silent invalidators': identical underlying data serialized in a different key/element order produces different prefix bytes → different cache key → guaranteed miss with no error surfaced. Fix: json.dumps(d, sort_keys=True) on every dumps call that lands above a breakpoint, and sort tool definitions by name before sending.
providers: Anthropic (mechanism is provider-agnostic for any prefix-cache scheme)
savings: UNQUANTIFIED (this is a necessary condition for any hit, not a marginal optimization)
effort: trivial — one flag, one sort call
trap: Python dict insertion-order (3.7+) hides the problem in single-process testing while the same code run across worker processes/restarts, or fed from a set literal, or fed from a DB query without ORDER BY, silently reintroduces it in production — the exact failure mode is invisible in local dev.

name: 4-breakpoint budget algorithm (system=1, last-tool=1, message window shrinks to fit remainder)
mechanism: FIXED bug, BlockRunAI/Franklin#73: naive breakpoint placement (system + last tool + last 3 messages = 5) exceeds Anthropic's hard 4-breakpoint cap, throwing HTTP 400 as soon as a tool-use session accumulates 3+ turns. Fix hard-budgets MAX_BREAKPOINTS=4, decrementing available slots as system (if present, -1) and tools (if present, -1) are consumed, then computes windowSize = min(3, max(0, 4 - used)) for the trailing message window — so the window shrinks from 3 to 2 messages exactly when system+tool already consumed 2 slots.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — this is a correctness fix (avoids outright request failure), not a cost optimization
effort: low — the exact JS is in the issue, ~15 lines
trap: Any hand-rolled breakpoint placement that assumes a fixed window size (e.g. always mark the last 3 messages) without accounting for how many slots system+tools already consumed will intermittently 400 exactly when tool use enters the conversation — the fixed-size-window bug is invisible until a session crosses the tool-use threshold, so it typically ships and passes initial testing.

name: TTL-promotion-before-reordering pipeline fix (preserve 1h TTL against silent downgrade)
mechanism: FIXED bug, router-for-me/CLIProxyAPI#3398: cache-control repair logic injected default (TTL-less, i.e. implicit 5m) ephemeral blocks, then ran ordering-normalization (which enforces Anthropic's tools→system→messages evaluation order) *before* any 1h-TTL blocks were promoted — so normalization would see a 1h block appearing after a remaining 5m-equivalent default block and downgrade/strip it. Fix reorders the pipeline: inject → enforce max-4 → explicitly promote any TTL-less/'5m' block to 'ttl:1h' when context supports it → re-run ordering normalization *after* promotion → sign.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — fixes silent regression from requested 1h TTL to actual 5m TTL, which changes cache-write cost multiplier (2x vs 1.25x) and retention window
effort: medium — requires re-sequencing an existing multi-stage request pipeline, not a single flag
trap: Pipeline ordering bugs like this are exactly the kind of thing that pass every 'does cache_control get sent' smoke test — the field IS present with ttl:'1h' at injection time, it just gets silently overwritten two stages later, so naive verification (log the outgoing request pre-pipeline) would show it working when the wire request does not.

name: InputTokensDetails.cache_write_tokens required-field compatibility shim
mechanism: FIXED bug, openai/openai-agents-python#3772: openai-python 2.45.0 made cache_write_tokens a required field on InputTokensDetails; openai-agents-python's Usage() default factory and ~10 other construction sites only set cached_tokens=0, so every fresh install combining agents 0.18.0 + openai 2.45.0 crashed at Runner.run() entry before any API call — a pure dependency-pinning break, not a caching-logic bug. Fix added cache_write_tokens=0 at all ~10 sites.
savings: N/A — availability fix
effort: N/A (already fixed upstream)
trap: Illustrates a general class of trap: any tool that constructs the SDK's own usage/cache-accounting types by hand (rather than round-tripping the SDK's returned object) is exposed to breaking on every upstream SDK schema addition to that type, even when the addition is caching-metadata-only and semantically a no-op for that integration.

name: Model-capability gate instead of hard-coded model-ID allowlist for enabling cache_control
mechanism: PROPOSED fix (not confirmed merged), Zoo-Code-Org/Zoo-Code#717: cache_control was attached only inside two hard-coded switch(modelId) allowlists; any cacheable Claude model whose exact literal ID wasn't enumerated fell to a default branch sending zero cache_control, silently disabling caching (cache_creation/read both 0, no error) for every new model release until someone manually added it to both switches. Proposed fix: replace both switches with a single `if (info.supportsPromptCache)` capability check against the existing ModelInfo flag already maintained for every model.
providers: Anthropic (via any router that maintains its own model catalog)
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — recovers 100% of caching for any newly-released model until the codebase is manually updated
effort: low — swap allowlist checks for one capability-flag check
trap: This is a maintenance-debt trap that recurs on every new model release: the router works perfectly for models known at the time the allowlist was written, then silently degrades to zero caching (with no error, just $0 in the console.anthropic.com cache columns) for every model shipped afterward, until a human notices the bill and files an issue.

name: Model-specific minimum-cacheable-prefix-length awareness (Haiku needs a longer prefix than Sonnet/Opus)
mechanism: Anthropic's docs specify a per-model minimum token count below which a marked breakpoint silently does not cache (cache_creation_input_tokens: 0, no error) rather than erroring. Per the anthropics/skills doc fetched: 512 tokens (Opus 5/Fable 5/Mythos 5), 1024 tokens (Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6/4.5, Opus 4.1/4), 2048 tokens (Opus 4.7, Mythos Preview, Haiku 3.5), 4096 tokens (Opus 4.6/4.5, Haiku 4.5). Independently corroborated by two separate practitioner bug reports (zeroclaw#3977, openclaw#69471) both observing 0% cache hit rate specifically on Haiku 4.5 while other models on the same gateway hit 44-71% — consistent with a prompt that clears Sonnet's threshold but not Haiku's higher one.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED
effort: trivial to check, but requires knowing the exact current per-model number, which changes across model generations
trap: Because the API returns zero cache tokens rather than an error, teams that switch cost-sensitive traffic to a cheaper model (e.g. Sonnet→Haiku) can silently lose 100% of their caching if their stable-prefix length was tuned to clear only the larger model's lower threshold — I did not independently re-verify these exact numbers against the live platform.claude.com docs, only against the single skills-repo doc I fetched, so treat the specific figures as needing a cross-check before being operationalized.

name: Bedrock cache-dialect translation (Anthropic cache_control ↔ Bedrock Converse cachePoint)
mechanism: CONFIRMED bug (unresolved at fetch time), cline/cline#12913: a routing layer emitted cache_control:{type:'ephemeral'} (Anthropic-direct dialect) via providerOptions, but the bundled @ai-sdk/amazon-bedrock package's convert-to-bedrock-chat-messages.ts only reads providerMetadata.bedrock.cachePoint (Bedrock Converse-API dialect) via its getCachePoint() function — reporter confirmed via binary grep of the built artifact: exactly 2 occurrences of 'cachePoint', both in the SDK's reader, zero writers anywhere in the 83MB binary. Net effect: caching silently never engages for any Bedrock-routed Claude call through that stack, with 100% of traffic paying full input price.
providers: Anthropic via AWS Bedrock, through Vercel AI SDK's amazon-bedrock provider
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — 100% of would-be cache benefit lost
effort: N/A — requires the AI SDK's Bedrock provider (or the calling app) to translate cache_control into cachePoint, not fixable from the app layer alone without a shim
trap: This is the general 'dialect mismatch across an abstraction boundary' failure mode — the writer and reader of cache metadata each independently support caching correctly for their own direct API, but nothing translates between them at the seam, and neither side errors.

name: cache_read_input_tokens → OpenAI-standard prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens normalization gap
mechanism: OPEN bug, BerriAI/litellm#27763: when Anthropic-format requests (with cache_control) are routed through LiteLLM to Vertex AI or Bedrock via /v1/messages passthrough, the upstream correctly returns Anthropic-native cache_read_input_tokens/cache_creation_input_tokens and caching genuinely works — but LiteLLM's Prometheus integration (_increment_cache_metrics in litellm/integrations/prometheus.py) only reads the OpenAI-standardized usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens field, which the /v1/messages passthrough path never populates. Result: litellm_cached_tokens_metric_total and litellm_cache_hits_metric_total never increment despite confirmed real cache hits.
providers: Anthropic via Vertex AI or Bedrock, through LiteLLM's /v1/messages passthrough + Prometheus integration
savings: N/A — this is an observability gap, not a caching failure; the underlying cost savings ARE occurring, only invisible in dashboards
effort: N/A — requires a LiteLLM-side fix (unresolved as of issue close date May 12, 2026)
trap: Teams using litellm_cached_tokens_metric_total as their source of truth for 'is caching working' would conclude caching is broken and go chase a phantom bug, when the actual billing-level caching is fine and only the metrics pipeline is blind. This is the inverse of a silent cache miss — a silent metrics miss masking a real hit.

name: Anthropic API usage-object cache accounting (input_tokens / cache_creation_input_tokens / cache_read_input_tokens, plus ephemeral_5m/1h split)
mechanism: The canonical measurement primitive underlying every tool above: usage.cache_creation_input_tokens (tokens newly written to cache this call, billed ~1.25x for 5m / ~2x for 1h), usage.cache_read_input_tokens (served from cache, ~0.1x), usage.input_tokens (full price, uncached), and usage.cache_creation.{ephemeral_5m_input_tokens, ephemeral_1h_input_tokens} which reveals which TTL regime the server actually applied to a given write — independent of, and sometimes contradicting, what TTL the client requested (see the ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H entry below). Total prompt size = sum of all three top-level fields. hit_rate = cache_read / (cache_read + cache_creation + input) is the standard rollup formula used consistently across cache-refund, cachebench, and the tianpan.co methodology.
savings: N/A — measurement primitive
effort: trivial — already returned on every response
trap: If cache_read_input_tokens is 0 on a request you expected to hit, you have proof of a miss but zero information about which of the many documented causes (TTL expiry, dynamic content, model-ID gating, dialect mismatch, sub-minimum prefix length, breakpoint-budget overflow, etc.) caused it — the field tells you THAT it missed, never WHY.

name: Server-side TTL override / 1h-TTL-requested-but-5m-TTL-billed (Claude Code, API-key auth)
mechanism: CLOSED bug (closed as a server-side issue, not a client bug), anthropics/claude-code#49139: client sent fully correct 1h-TTL request shape — system/message blocks with cache_control:{type:'ephemeral', ttl:'1h', scope:'global'} and the prompt-caching-scope-2026-01-05 beta header — yet the server response showed cache_creation:{ephemeral_5m_input_tokens: 7025, ephemeral_1h_input_tokens: 0}: all tokens landed in the 5-minute bucket regardless. Reproduced on Claude Code 2.1.110, Windows, both enterprise/org and personal API keys.
savings: N/A — this is a cost-increasing server anomaly (forces 5m re-caching cadence instead of the requested 1h), not a savings technique
effort: N/A — not client-fixable; issue was closed without the underlying cause being disclosed in what I could retrieve
trap: The issue closure only says 'server-side API issue' with no further technical detail — I cannot determine from what's available whether this was a one-off outage, a specific-header/org-config edge case, or a broader current-gen phenomenon. This affects only cache retention duration (more frequent full-price re-writes), not what the model receives on a hit, so on the tier axis it's Tier A by definition — but I'm marking the finding itself 'unknown' because I could not confirm whether it is still reproducible today (Aug 2026) or was already resolved server-side by the time of closure. Settling this needs a live repro: send an identical 1h-TTL request twice with a few-minute gap and check whether ephemeral_1h_input_tokens is ever nonzero.

name: Dynamic system-prompt content as cache killer (timestamps, message IDs, session metadata)
mechanism: CONFIRMED with dollar evidence, openclaw/openclaw#19534: system prompt contained a 'Current Date & Time' section plus message IDs/session metadata that changed every turn, so the prefix-match cache (which requires exact byte identity) rebuilt from scratch on every single call. Reporter measured expected ~$0.05/message post-cache-write vs actual ~$0.50/message, i.e. $9 expected vs $35 actual in one day — roughly the 1.25x-write-vs-0.1x-read gap compounding over a full session with zero reuse.
providers: Anthropic (mechanism applies to any prefix-cache provider)
savings: practitioner-reported ~7x real-world cost inflation ($9→$35/day) attributable to this single cause
effort: low once identified — move the dynamic section after the last cache_control breakpoint, or drop it if non-essential — but the issue itself was closed with 'No response'/no fix documented at time of report
trap: This is the single most-repeated root cause across every tool and issue I found (cache-audit rule 1, prompt-cache-doctor's primary detection, claude-code-cache-fix's fingerprint-strip, and this issue independently) — teams keep re-discovering it because a 'current date' or 'session ID' field feels harmless and rarely gets code-reviewed as a cost issue.

name: claude-code-cache-fix proxy pipeline (sort-stabilization, fingerprint-strip, identity-normalization)
mechanism: Practitioner-diagnosed 3-cause regression on resumed Claude Code sessions: (1) attachment blocks meant to live in messages[0] drift to later messages on resume, shifting the cache prefix; (2) a cc_version fingerprint computed from message content shifts when those blocks relocate, changing the system prompt bytes; (3) tool definitions arrive in non-deterministic order between turns. Fix proxy applies sort-stabilization (deterministic tool/MCP ordering — this part is Tier A, same content, same order every time), fingerprint-strip (removes the unstable cc_version field from the system prompt entirely), and identity-normalization. Self-reported 95.5% cache hit rate through the proxy vs 82.3% direct.
savings: practitioner-reported 95.5% vs 82.3% hit rate delta, single-source, not independently audited
effort: medium — runs as an intercepting proxy in front of Claude Code
trap: sort-stabilization is a straightforward Tier A fix (reordering doesn't change model input semantics). But fingerprint-strip REMOVES a content field the model would otherwise see — that is a Tier C change (different input reaches the model) masquerading as a caching fix, and the README excerpt I could retrieve does not address whether the stripped cc_version field carries any information the model's behavior depends on. This is exactly the kind of 'fix' that could silently alter model behavior while appearing to only affect cost — I flag it unknown/needs-experiment rather than folding it into the Tier A sort-stabilization finding, and would not ship it without A/B-testing model output with the field present vs stripped.

name: Provider-specific beta-header dialect mismatch across gateways (Anthropic-direct header rejected by Vertex/OpenRouter/etc.)
mechanism: CONFIRMED regression, Aider-AI/aider#2961: aider 0.72.1 unconditionally sent anthropic-beta: prompt-caching-2024-07-31 to Claude 3.5 Sonnet even when routed through VertexAI, which rejects that header value outright ('Unexpected value(s) ... for the anthropic-beta header'), breaking every request through that path (not just caching — the whole call 400s). Downgrading to 0.71.0 was the only workaround; root cause (send the beta header unconditionally regardless of backend) was not fixed in the content I could retrieve.
providers: Anthropic (direct) vs Vertex AI-fronted Claude, via LiteLLM/Aider's routing layer
savings: N/A — availability-breaking, not a cost-savings item
effort: N/A — requires backend-aware conditional header logic in the calling tool, unresolved as documented
trap: A caching-enablement change (adding the beta header) broke non-caching functionality entirely on a subset of backends — the two concerns (does caching work, does the request work at all) are coupled at the header level and a naive 'add prompt caching support' PR can regress availability for every user on an indirect backend.

name: Async/batch billing path — 50% discount vs synchronous API, same model & weights
mechanism: Requests are submitted as a job (file or inline array) instead of a synchronous call; the provider schedules the identical forward pass whenever capacity allows within a target SLA window and writes results to a retrievable store instead of streaming them back live. Model, weights, and decoding params are unchanged — only the transport/scheduling/billing path differs.
savings: 50% off standard per-token pricing, confirmed independently in each provider's own docs: Anthropic ("50% cost discount at scale"), OpenAI ("50% cost discount compared to synchronous APIs"), Gemini ("50% of the standard cost"), Bedrock ("50% lower price compared to on-demand inference pricing"). All four land on the identical 50% figure.
effort: low-medium: requires JSONL/array construction, a submit+poll (or webhook) loop, and tolerance for a ~24h SLA window (Bedrock's window is configurable via timeoutDurationInHours; the other three are fixed at 24h). Non-streaming only — no partial/incremental output.
trap: Latency-tolerance is a hard requirement, not a suggestion — none of the four guarantee sub-24h turnaround (Gemini explicitly says 24h target, 'often quicker' but not promised). Chunking limits differ sharply and silently truncate oversized jobs if not respected: OpenAI 50,000 requests/200MB file; Gemini 20MB inline / 2GB file; Anthropic ~100,000 items/256MB (see openQuestions — this number comes from a third-party code comment, not verified against current platform.claude.com docs in this pass); Bedrock has no fixed published request-count cap but real jobs were observed to fail validation above ~40GB total input despite a larger nominal quota (aws-samples orchestrator sets its byte budget from a conservative 5GB-per-cohort default, not the nominal ceiling).

name: In-flight request coalescing (N concurrent identical requests → 1 forward pass, N-1 free)
mechanism: Before issuing a call, hash the full request (must include model+temperature+max_tokens+tools+system, not just the message content) and check a registry of currently-executing requests keyed by that hash. If a match is in flight, block on it (an asyncio.Future, a threading.Event, or a Redis SET NX + poll) and return its eventual result to every waiter instead of issuing a second call. This is not a cache replay — it's N callers sharing literally the same live forward pass, so it is unconditionally output-identical for every waiter including at temperature>0 (they all get the one sample that was actually drawn).
providers: provider-agnostic — sits in front of any of the four APIs
savings: Inferred, not measured in any source found: eliminates 100% of the cost of every concurrent duplicate beyond the first. No source publishes a fleet-wide dollar or percentage figure — the real-world saving is entirely a function of how often your traffic actually produces exact concurrent duplicates (fan-out races, retried UI clicks, multi-agent redundancy), which none of these repos benchmark.
effort: low: a hash map + lock/Future is ~50-150 LOC; the Redis variant (cross-process) is similarly small.
trap: The dedup key must hash EVERY parameter that affects the forward pass. Jcstack/ashare-ai-analyst's implementation hashes only `messages` (visible in the code) — if model or temperature differ between two 'concurrent' calls, this design would silently serve caller B the response to caller A's different request. That is exactly the wrong-A-costs-the-customer failure mode the brief warns about: get the key wrong and you've turned a Tier-A optimization into an undetectable Tier-C correctness bug. Also: an in-flight request that itself fails/times out must propagate the error to all waiters (not just the caller who happened to originate it) or waiters will hang or silently retry into a second real call.

name: AWS Bedrock CreateModelInvocationJob clientRequestToken — provider-native idempotent job creation
mechanism: Bedrock's batch job creation API accepts an optional clientRequestToken parameter (the standard AWS idempotency-token pattern, same family as EC2's). Retrying the create call with the same token returns the existing job instead of creating a second one — this is enforced server-side by AWS, not something the caller has to build.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — prevents double-billing of an entire batch job on a client-side retry-after-ambiguous-failure, but the frequency of that event (and thus the dollar value) isn't published anywhere.
effort: trivial: pass one extra string parameter you already generate (e.g. a UUID derived from your own job's content hash).
trap: This is the ONLY one of the four providers with native, documented idempotent batch-job creation. Anthropic's Batches.create has no metadata/idempotency parameter at all (confirmed both in platform.claude.com's request-body reference and in a third-party SDK adapter's design notes); OpenAI's Batch API docs make no mention of idempotency keys; and Google's Gemini Batch Mode docs say outright: 'The creation of a batch job is not idempotent. If you send the same creation request twice, two separate batch jobs will be created.' Anyone porting a Bedrock-shaped retry pattern to the other three providers without adding a client-side dedup layer will double-submit and double-pay on every ambiguous network failure during job creation.

name: Client-side idempotency-key gateway — cache-and-replay for exact-duplicate synchronous calls
mechanism: A proxy sits in front of the provider API. On each request the client supplies an Idempotency-Key header. The gateway does an atomic Redis SET NX on that key: first caller 'owns' it and proceeds, storing the complete response under the key on success; a caller with a key already resolved gets the stored response verbatim (no upstream call); a caller whose key is still in-flight gets a 409/DuplicateInFlight signal to wait or back off.
providers: provider-agnostic wrapper — reference implementation targets OpenAI
savings: Inferred: 100% of the upstream cost is saved on every exact-duplicate replay (same key, e.g. from a flaky-network client retry). No measured hit-rate published.
effort: low-medium: needs a Redis (or equivalent KV with atomic CAS) instance and a TTL policy; the reference implementation explicitly only caches non-streaming JSON responses and passes streaming through untouched.
trap: Per the product's own Tier-B definition: at temperature > 0 this freezes one historical sample and serves it to every future retry with that key instead of drawing a fresh one. That's a real behavioral change a caller might not expect from something billed as 'just retry safety.' Also note the key is CLIENT-supplied — the gateway has no way to verify the key actually corresponds to the request body attached to it (the reference implementation doesn't appear to validate key-to-body binding), which is a spoofing/collision risk if the key namespace isn't scoped per-caller.

name: Local idempotency ledger over a non-idempotent Batches.create (submit-time dedup + crash-recovery reconciliation)
mechanism: Since Anthropic's Batches API has no server-side idempotency mechanism, submit() takes a caller-owned idempotency_key and a known_refs map (key -> BatchRef); if the key is already present, the existing ref is returned with zero API calls. The idempotency key is separately stamped into the batch's metadata via extra_body (working around the typed SDK's create() having no metadata parameter) so that on process crash, find_batch() can scan the most recent batches (bounded to the last 200) and match on that stamped key to recover the ref without re-submitting — turning an at-least-once orchestrator (crash between create() and the caller's own event log write) into an effectively-once one.
providers: Anthropic Message Batches (pattern is portable to OpenAI/Gemini, which have the identical non-idempotent-create gap)
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — avoids paying for a second full batch job (up to 100,000 items) on exactly the crash window between 'batch created' and 'we recorded that fact', which without this pattern is a silent double-bill with no error to catch it.
effort: medium: requires an event log or durable known_refs store the caller owns, plus willingness to smuggle data through extra_body since the typed SDK doesn't expose a batch-level metadata field.
trap: The bounded scan (200 most recent batches) is a real limit — it assumes an orphaned batch is always near the head of the provider's batch-list ordering, which breaks under high submission concurrency across many workers/tenants sharing one API key. Also: this whole pattern exists only because Anthropic doesn't support it natively; it needs to be re-verified against current docs periodically since providers do add idempotency support (Bedrock already has it) and a hand-rolled workaround can silently become redundant-but-harmless, or worse, conflict with a newly-added native mechanism.

name: Conditional-write claim/revert state machine for exactly-once-over-at-least-once batch orchestration, with budget-bounded chunking and pre-SIGKILL deadline guards
mechanism: A DynamoDB-backed STAGING -> IN_FLIGHT -> DONE/FAILED state machine where every transition is a single conditional UpdateItem (ConditionExpression checks current status, optionally also batchJobId). This makes every step idempotent under Step Functions' at-least-once retry semantics: a re-run of a 'claim' no-ops on already-claimed records; a re-run of a 'revert' no-ops on records already reverted or re-claimed by a newer job. Chunking is budget-bounded per shard (both a record-count target AND a cumulative-byte budget, whichever binds first, since Bedrock's real per-job size ceiling was observed well below its nominal quota), with page-level overshoot capped to at most one record over budget rather than one whole page. A materialize worker derives its output filename from a hash of its own record IDs (content-stable across retries) so a retried worker overwrites its own file instead of duplicating records. A 90-second deadline guard proactively reverts unfinished claims before Lambda's hard SIGKILL, because the exception handler that would normally revert them never runs on a kill signal — this closes a specific observed failure mode (records stranded IN_FLIGHT forever). Fetch-failure retries and inference-attempt retries are tracked as SEPARATE budgets (fetchFailCount vs retryCount) so a transient S3 blip doesn't consume the same retry allowance as a real inference failure.
providers: AWS Bedrock batch inference (orchestration layer built on top; pattern is provider-agnostic)
savings: UNQUANTIFIED in dollar terms — the design doc frames the payoff as avoiding stranded/duplicate work at scale (explicitly cites a 100k-record job that used to time out scanning millions of unrelated rows before the manifest-based revert path was added: O(job) instead of O(backlog)), not as a measured cost reduction.
effort: high: this is a full Step Functions + DynamoDB + Lambda orchestration layer (~1000+ LOC across claim/materialize/revert handlers), appropriate only at a scale where a hand-rolled poll loop stops being reliable.
trap: This is the most sophisticated failure-handling reference found in this sweep, and it is that sophisticated specifically because the naive version breaks in production at scale: unbounded GSI scans for revert don't finish before their own timeout at high backlog depth; batch cohorts silently exceed a provider's REAL (not nominal) size ceiling; and Lambda's SIGKILL-on-timeout bypasses ordinary exception-handling cleanup. Anyone building a lighter-weight batch orchestrator should treat each of these as a named failure mode to test for, not assume 'we have retries' covers it.

name: Cancel generation on client disconnect (SSE stream abandonment / non-streaming abandonment)
mechanism: For self-hosted inference (confirmed): the server polls the ASGI request's is_disconnected() during both streaming (between SSE frames) and non-streaming (FastAPI/uvicorn does NOT auto-cancel a handler coroutine on disconnect, so this must be done manually) requests, and cancels the underlying generation task the moment a disconnect is detected — freeing the GPU/scheduler slot instead of letting inference run to completion for output nobody will ever see. A background reaper also sweeps 'orphaned collectors' whose consumer coroutine never got to run its own cleanup (e.g. the client disconnected before the SSE stream even began). For hosted, per-token-billed APIs (Anthropic/OpenAI/Gemini): whether closing the HTTP connection client-side actually stops the provider from generating (and billing for) further output tokens is NOT established by any source found in this pass — I could not locate a primary doc statement either way, and the web-search budget for this session was exhausted before I could chase community reports down. This is exactly a case the brief says to tag 'unknown' rather than default to A.
providers: Anthropic/OpenAI/Gemini hosted APIs (mechanism unverified for hosted billing)
savings: UNQUANTIFIED for self-hosted (no GPU-hour benchmark published in the repo); completely unknown for hosted APIs pending the experiment below.
effort: low-medium for self-hosted (a disconnect-poll wrapper around the streaming/non-streaming response path, ~100 LOC as shown); effort for hosted is moot until the billing behavior is confirmed.
trap: Even in the confirmed self-hosted case, the repo's own comments document an inherent detection-lag window: 'uvicorn's ASGI disconnect message is not delivered until after the generator yields,' so during long prefill (their example: 90k tokens) compute keeps burning for some unavoidable interval even with best-effort polling — this is a floor on how much waste this technique can eliminate, not a full fix. THE EXPERIMENT THAT WOULD SETTLE THE HOSTED-API QUESTION: issue a streaming request for a long completion, forcibly close the TCP connection partway through (not a graceful stream-end), wait, then query the provider's usage/billing endpoint for that request — if output_tokens reflects the FULL generation the model would have produced, disconnect-abort saves nothing on hosted APIs; if it reflects only tokens generated up to the moment of disconnect (and generation genuinely stopped early), the self-hosted pattern above ports directly and is a real Tier-A-adjacent saving (aborting compute the customer was never going to consume, at zero output impact since there was no consumer).

name: SDK-generated idempotency key that is never actually transmitted (dead code, not a real protection)
mechanism: Both the official anthropic-sdk-python and openai-python base clients generate a per-request idempotency key (`f"stainless-python-retry-{uuid.uuid4()}"`) and reuse it across the SDK's own internal retries of a single logical call (network-error / 5xx retries, not user-initiated resubmission). This LOOKS like exactly the Tier-A retry-safety mechanism the brief is asking about. But `self._idempotency_header` is hardwired to `None` in `__init__` in BOTH SDKs' `_base_client.py`, and a full repo-wide code search in both repos found NO other assignment to it anywhere — meaning the generated key is computed, stored on the request options, and then never attached as an HTTP header, because the header-injection code (`if idempotency_header and options.idempotency_key ...`) short-circuits on the always-None header name. Corroborated by both providers' own docs: neither documents idempotency-key support on the Messages/Chat-Completions endpoints (OpenAI's Idempotency-Key header IS documented and functional, but only for its separate Agentic Commerce API, not core generation).
savings: 0% — the mechanism provides no actual deduplication. Any product or user assuming 'the official SDK retries safely because it uses idempotency keys' is relying on a protection that does not exist for these endpoints as of this code.
effort: N/A — this is a finding about existing tooling's absence of protection, not a technique to adopt.
trap: This is precisely the 'wrong A costs us the customer' scenario the brief warns against: it would be easy to read the SDK source, see idempotency-key generation and reuse-across-retries, and catalogue it as a working Tier-A safety net — it is not one. The actual consequence: when the SDK's built-in retry logic fires (e.g., on a read-timeout where the server had, in fact, already completed and would have returned the full generation), the retry is a genuinely new, separately-billed forward pass with no server-side collapsing — this is a real, currently-unmitigated instance of exactly the 'timeouts that abandon a completed generation' wasted-spend category the brief calls under-explored. A product wanting to fix this must build its own request-hash-based dedup layer (Tier B — freezes one sample at temperature>0, per the product's own tier rules) since neither provider offers a server-side alternative for these endpoints today.

name: Anthropic Prompt Caching (cache_control breakpoints, automatic mode)
mechanism: Exact-match prefix caching: identical leading tokens (system prompt, tool defs, documents) up to a cache_control breakpoint reuse the previously computed KV cache instead of recomputing. Same forward pass for the cached span; only the compute path and billing differ.
savings: Cache read = 0.1x base input price (90% discount). Cache write = 1.25x base (5-min TTL) or 2.0x base (1-hour TTL). Min cacheable length 512-4096 tokens depending on model.
effort: low — add one cache_control field per request; no infra change
trap: The 90% figure is the read discount only; if your prefix churns faster than the TTL you pay 1.25-2x write premiums more often than you collect 0.1x reads, and net cost goes up. Also: this is opt-in per-request, not automatic, so a naive integration gets zero benefit.
stillCurrent: Yes, current as of Aug 2026 docs check this session; Anthropic is the only one of the three majors making an explicit unconditional output-identity guarantee in writing.

name: OpenAI Automatic Prompt Caching
mechanism: Same exact-prefix KV-cache-reuse mechanism as Anthropic's, applied automatically (no opt-in) above a 1024-token prefix, in 128-token increments.
savings: Discount varies by model: gpt-4o 50%, gpt-4.1 75%, gpt-5-nano/gpt-5.2 90%, gpt-realtime (audio) 98.75%. Confirmed from OpenAI's own cookbook pricing table.
effort: none — fully automatic above the token threshold; the only action is structuring prompts so static content is a shared, byte-identical prefix
trap: OpenAI's docs explicitly refuse to guarantee output identity: caching doesn't change generation, but 'otherwise identical nondeterministic requests are not guaranteed to return identical output' — a materially weaker claim than Anthropic's. Discount also varies 50-90% by model generation, so a blanket '90% savings' pitch is wrong for gpt-4o-class models.
stillCurrent: Yes, verified this session against developers.openai.com and the cookbook.

name: Google Gemini Context Caching (implicit + explicit)
mechanism: Implicit caching (default, on for all Gemini 2.5+ models) automatically detects repeated prefixes; explicit caching lets the customer pin a cache object with a TTL and pay storage cost for guaranteed availability. Same KV-cache-reuse mechanism.
savings: 90% discount on cached tokens for Gemini 2.5+, 75% for Gemini 2.0. Implicit caching has no storage cost; explicit caching bills storage separately. Min prefix 2048 tokens on 2.5 Flash/Pro.
effort: none for implicit; low (create a CachedContent object) for explicit
trap: I could not find explicit output-identity language on ai.google.dev comparable to Anthropic's — the page I fetched didn't address it either way. Don't assume parity with Anthropic's written guarantee until you find the specific sentence; treat as 'presumed A by mechanism, unconfirmed by doc language' pending a follow-up fetch.
stillCurrent: Partially verified — pricing/thresholds confirmed, output-identity claim not found in the page fetched this session.

name: PagedAttention / vLLM
mechanism: Paged, non-contiguous KV-cache memory management (OS-paging analogy) that eliminates fragmentation and enables block-level sharing across requests with identical prefixes. Reused blocks are literal stored KV bytes, not recomputed.
savings: 2-4x throughput vs FasterTransformer/Orca baselines; 6.1-9.8% KV memory savings on parallel sampling, 37.6-55.2% on beam search (OPT-13B, Alpaca trace).
effort: high if self-hosting (deploy vLLM); zero if only using a hosted API that happens to run it under the hood
trap: Customer-actionable only if you self-host or if your provider exposes the underlying engine choice. If you're calling OpenAI/Anthropic/Google's hosted API you have zero visibility into whether this is running — it's fully provider-internal and already priced into whatever they charge.
stillCurrent: Yes, vLLM is still the dominant open-source serving engine as of Aug 2026.

name: RadixAttention / SGLang
mechanism: Generalizes prefix caching beyond simple prefix match: maintains an LRU radix tree of all requests' KV caches, enabling automatic multi-level sharing (few-shot examples, agent templates, branching conversations), not just a single linear prefix.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED from what I directly verified — reported throughput/latency gains in the original blog/paper but I did not pull a specific number I could stand behind; treat any '5x' or '6x' figure you see elsewhere as unverified until checked against the paper directly.
effort: high if self-hosting; zero visibility if only calling a hosted API on top of it
trap: Same actionability trap as PagedAttention — provider-internal unless you deploy SGLang yourself.

name: Hydragen
mechanism: Hardware-aware exact attention decomposition: splits attention computation into a shared-prefix component (batched across all sequences as matrix-matrix ops) and a unique-suffix component, replacing memory-bound matrix-vector products with compute-efficient matrix-matrix products. Exact, not approximate.
providers: Research prototype (Stanford Scaling Intelligence lab); no confirmed commercial hosted deployment
savings: 3x CodeLlama-13B throughput at 1K shared prefix, 30x+ at 16K prefix, batch size 1K on 8xA100 (ICML 2024).
effort: high — requires custom kernel integration, self-hosted only
trap: Category (iii) only — no evidence this shipped in any hosted API as of this search. Good citation for 'the literature has solved this,' bad citation for 'you can turn this on today.'
stillCurrent: Mechanism still valid; production adoption unconfirmed.

name: ChunkAttention
mechanism: Prefix-aware KV cache broken into chunks organized in a prefix tree, with a two-phase-partition attention kernel that improves data locality when many concurrent requests share a system prompt.
providers: Microsoft (research, ACL 2024); no confirmed commercial hosted deployment identified
savings: 3.2-4.8x self-attention kernel speedup; peak KV cache memory dropped from 14.79GB to 3.28GB (~78% reduction) for 1024-4096 token shared system prompts.
effort: high — self-hosted only
trap: Same as Hydragen — real technique, no verified hosted-API exposure.

name: AttentionStore / CachedAttention
mechanism: Persists KV caches across multi-turn conversation turns in a hierarchical (GPU/CPU/disk) storage system instead of discarding them at turn end, avoiding recomputation when a session resumes.
providers: Research (USENIX ATC'24); provider affiliation not independently confirmed in this pass
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — I did not pull a specific throughput/latency number from a source I trust for this session; the paper reports gains but I flag this as unverified rather than guess a figure.
effort: high — self-hosted, requires a hierarchical cache tier
trap: Same actionability ceiling — this is what makes multi-turn chat products cheap for the provider, invisible and non-configurable to the API customer.

name: Mooncake (KVCache-centric disaggregated serving)
mechanism: Separates prefill and decode into different clusters and uses a KVCache-centric scheduler plus CPU/DRAM/SSD tiers of the GPU cluster as a disaggregated KV cache, maximizing effective throughput under SLOs.
savings: Up to 525% throughput increase in simulated long-context scenarios vs baseline; 59-498% effective capacity increase on real production traces. Self-reported: 100B+ tokens/day across thousands of nodes.
effort: very high — this is a full serving-architecture rebuild, not a knob
trap: This is the clearest evidence that provider-internal serving architecture is where the big multiples live — but it's Moonshot's own paper about Moonshot's own system, so the numbers are self-reported, not third-party audited. Zero customer actionability through any public API.
stillCurrent: Yes, actively described as in production.

name: LMCache
mechanism: Extracts KV caches from vLLM/SGLang and makes them persistent and shareable across serving engine instances (both prefix-reuse offloading and prefill-decode disaggregation), rather than tied to a single engine's memory.
providers: LMCache (open source, UChicago-affiliated, same lineage as CacheGen/CacheBlend authors); integrates with NVIDIA Dynamo KVBM
savings: Up to 15x throughput improvement combined with vLLM (self-reported tech report).
effort: high — self-hosted infra layer
trap: This is the one entry in this KV-reuse cluster that a token-spread customer COULD deploy themselves if they self-host, making it category (iii)-but-reachable rather than pure (ii). Still requires running your own vLLM/SGLang stack, not a hosted-API call.
stillCurrent: Yes, actively developed, tech report is 2025.

name: Prompt Cache (Yale/Google, MLSys 2024)
mechanism: Defines reusable 'prompt modules' with a schema that preserves positional accuracy, precomputing and reusing attention states for frequently-recurring text segments (not just linear prefixes).
providers: Research prototype (Yale + Google); commercial descendants are the hosted prompt-caching features listed above
savings: TTFT reduced up to 8x on GPU, up to 60x on CPU, 'without compromising output accuracy' (paper's own framing).
effort: high if implementing the schema yourself; the commercial hosted-caching products are the actionable version
trap: This is the intellectual ancestor of Anthropic/OpenAI/Google's shipped features — good for citing where the idea came from, not itself something you can call today.
stillCurrent: Mechanism valid; superseded in practice by vendor-specific hosted implementations.

name: Continuous batching / iteration-level scheduling (Orca)
mechanism: Batches requests at the iteration (per-token) level rather than request level, with 'selective batching' applied only to compatible ops, letting new requests join a running batch without waiting for the whole batch to finish. Mathematically, each sequence's correct next-token distribution is unaffected by which other sequences share its batch.
providers: Orca (OSDI 2022, origin); vLLM, SGLang, TGI, TensorRT-LLM all implement variants; effectively universal in production serving
savings: 36.9x throughput vs FasterTransformer at matched latency, GPT-3 175B (Orca's own benchmark).
effort: zero customer action possible — pure provider-internal scheduling
trap: I initially defaulted this to Tier A ('same math, just reordered') and caught myself: the Thinking Machines batch-invariance work names dynamic/continuous batching specifically as the mechanism that breaks numerical determinism, because most GPU kernels (RMSNorm, matmul, attention) are NOT batch-invariant — the same mathematical operation returns different floating-point results depending on batch composition. So in exact arithmetic this is Tier A, but on real hardware with non-batch-invariant kernels it can measurably change individual outputs. Settling experiment: repeat a fixed prompt at T=0 under a provider's real production load (varying concurrent batch composition) vs. isolated/dedicated capacity, and diff outputs — this is essentially what Thinking Machines and the 152334H blog already did informally.
stillCurrent: Yes, continuous batching is standard; the batch-invariance fix is not yet confirmed shipped anywhere.

name: Speculative decoding, strict rejection sampling (Leviathan et al., ICML 2023)
mechanism: A small draft model proposes k tokens; the target model scores them in one parallel forward pass; a rejection-sampling step accepts/rejects each draft token such that the ACCEPTED SEQUENCE'S DISTRIBUTION IS PROVABLY IDENTICAL to sampling directly from the target model. This is a real, cited, mathematically proven result — a genuine Tier-A guarantee at the distributional level.
providers: Algorithm is open; production use at OpenAI/Anthropic/Google is neither confirmed nor denied in any primary source I found this session. Confirmed in use at inference-specialist providers: Fireworks (FireAttention), likely Groq/Together per secondary sources (not primary-doc confirmed).
savings: 2-3x decoding speedup in the original paper's benchmarks.
effort: zero customer action possible today — no hosted API exposes a toggle, and none publicly discloses whether it's running
trap: THE key distinction the brief asked for: the Leviathan proof guarantees the OUTPUT DISTRIBUTION matches target-only decoding — it does not guarantee that a single sampled run will be byte-identical to a single target-only run, because both are draws from a distribution. At temperature 0 you'd expect the argmax path to collapse to determinism, but a June 2026 arXiv study that actually measured this on real vLLM stacks (not just proved it on paper) found only 90.66% byte-identity (2592/2859 pairs) between strict-rejection-sampling speculative decoding and target-only decoding at T=0 — the gap traced to floating-point non-associativity in the verification step, the same root cause as the batch-invariance problem, NOT a flaw in the algorithm's proof. So: the mathematical guarantee is real and holds in expectation over the true distribution; the practical bit-for-bit guarantee does not survive real GPU kernels. Tag 'unknown' rather than A because a single customer-facing comparison (did my cached/replayed answer match what I'd get right now) is not covered by the proof. Settling experiment: exactly what 2606.25097 did, but run against actual hosted commercial APIs (OpenAI/Anthropic/Google) rather than self-hosted vLLM — nobody has published that yet.
stillCurrent: Proof still holds; empirical byte-identity finding is new (2026) and narrows the practical claim.

name: Speculative sampling (Chen et al., DeepMind, 2023)
mechanism: Independently-derived version of the same rejection-sampling speculative decoding idea, benchmarked on Chinchilla-70B in a distributed setting.
providers: DeepMind (algorithm); production deployment status not confirmed in any primary source found this session
savings: 2-2.5x decoding speedup without modifying the model or sample quality (paper's own framing — 'sample quality' again means distributional, see caveat above).
effort: zero customer action possible
trap: Same distributional-vs-byte-identical caveat as Leviathan et al. Also: I could not confirm a final peer-reviewed venue beyond arXiv for this specific paper in this session — treat venue as arXiv-preprint-only unless you verify otherwise.

name: Batch-invariant kernels (Thinking Machines Lab, 'Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference')
mechanism: Replaces RMSNorm, matmul, and attention kernels with versions whose output does not depend on batch size / batch composition, by using fixed-shape reduction strategies instead of load-adaptive ones. This is the actual fix for the root cause identified above.
providers: Thinking Machines Lab (open-source library + vLLM demo); no major hosted API (OpenAI/Anthropic/Google) confirmed to have adopted this in production as of this search
savings: Measured on Qwen3-235B: before fix, 1000 T=0 completions produced 80 unique outputs (divergence starting at token 103); after fix, all 1000 identical. This is a determinism result, not a cost-savings result — its business value is enabling reliable exact-match Tier-B caching and RL training stability, not direct inference cost reduction.
effort: very high — kernel-level rewrite, self-hosted only
trap: This is a provider-blog claim (Thinking Machines' own numbers), not independently peer-reviewed, though an independent blogger (Dogukan Tuna) reproduced the RMSNorm/matmul batch-invariant ops in JAX as a partial replication. No hosted API customer can invoke this; it matters to token-spread only as: (a) evidence for WHY temperature-0 hosted output isn't reproducible today, and (b) a thing to watch for if a provider announces adopting it, since that would upgrade their Tier-B response-cache reliability.
stillCurrent: Yes, published ~Nov 2025, still the reference result as of Aug 2026.

name: LLM-42 (Microsoft Research, decode-verify-rollback determinism)
mechanism: Runs the normal non-deterministic fast decoding path, then replays candidate tokens under a FIXED-SHAPE reduction schedule to verify consistency, committing only tokens 'guaranteed to be consistent across runs' and rolling back the rest — enforcing determinism without a full kernel rewrite.
providers: Microsoft Research (arXiv Jan 2026, open-source repo microsoft/llm-42); self-hosted only, no hosted-API adoption confirmed
savings: Overhead 'in proportion to the traffic that requires determinism' per the abstract — no specific throughput/latency percentage was available in what I could extract from the abstract; treat as UNQUANTIFIED pending a full-text read.
effort: very high, self-hosted, requires custom scheduling layer
trap: Very recent (Jan 2026) — not yet peer-reviewed at a venue as far as I could confirm; treat provenance as the authors' own technical report rather than vetted peer review until a venue is confirmed. Zero customer actionability through any hosted API.
stillCurrent: Yes, recent and directly on-topic for the determinism question.

name: Exact-match / byte-identical request-response caching (generic application-level pattern, no single canonical paper)
mechanism: Hash the full request (model, params, exact prompt bytes) and store the complete response; on an exact repeat request within a TTL, replay the stored response instead of calling the API at all. This is the 'B' tier as defined in the brief: safe only because the request is a true duplicate.
providers: Not a vendor product — implemented ad hoc by API consumers, or via gateway products (e.g., LLM proxy/gateway tools that offer 'response caching' as distinct from provider-side 'prompt caching')
savings: 100% of the request cost avoided on a hit (no model call at all) — the ceiling case, but only for genuinely repeated requests, which in practice is a small fraction of real traffic outside of test suites, demos, and idempotent tool calls.
effort: medium — build/operate a keyed cache layer (e.g., Redis) in front of the API call
trap: AT TEMPERATURE > 0, THIS FREEZES ONE HISTORICAL SAMPLE INSTEAD OF DRAWING A FRESH INDEPENDENT ONE — this is a behavioral change, not output-neutral, exactly as the brief specified must be tagged. It silently converts a stochastic-sampling product into a deterministic-lookup product for cached paths, which can matter for anything relying on response diversity (e.g., re-rolling for creative variance, self-consistency voting, or A/B-style sampling). At T=0 it is closer to safe in intent, but per the empirical findings above (152334H blog: 11.67/30 unique GPT-4 completions at T=0; ACM TOSEM peer-reviewed study confirming non-determinism persists at T=0 for GPT-3.5/4 code generation), even T=0 hosted output is NOT itself guaranteed reproducible run-to-run — so a cached T=0 response is not provably 'what you'd get right now' either, it's just 'what you got once.'
stillCurrent: Yes, this is an evergreen engineering pattern, not tied to any specific model generation.

name: OpenAI `seed` parameter (best-effort reproducibility control)
mechanism: Customer sets an integer seed plus identical other parameters; OpenAI attempts to route to the same numerical configuration. The response includes a system_fingerprint the customer can compare across calls to detect infra changes.
savings: Not a cost-savings lever — it's a determinism control. Relevant to the brief's explicit request for state-of-the-art on hosted determinism, not to the cost side of the product.
effort: low — pass one extra parameter
trap: OpenAI's own docs explicitly hedge: 'mostly identical,' 'small chance responses differ even when request parameters and system_fingerprint match, due to the inherent non-determinism of our models.' This is exactly a case where the provider itself refuses to claim Tier A or B — tag 'unknown' rather than assume the seed parameter delivers a real guarantee. I did not verify whether Anthropic or Google expose an equivalent parameter this session — open question below.

name: Anthropic prompt caching (cache_control breakpoints)
mechanism: cache_control marks a prefix; on an exact byte-identical repeat of that prefix, Anthropic reuses the stored KV-cache state instead of recomputing attention over it. Same model, same forward pass over the cached region — only compute-reuse and billing differ. Billed: cache reads ~10% of standard input rate, cache writes ~125% of standard input rate (a write premium).
savings: "up to 90% cost / up to 85% latency" per Anthropic's own posts; ProjectDiscovery (named practitioner, production system) reports 59% overall reduction, 66% post-optimization, 70% in their most recent 10 days, cache hit rate improved 7%→84%, 9.8B tokens served from cache
effort: low-medium — restructure prompt so static content is a fixed prefix, add cache_control breakpoints
trap: Below the per-model minimum cacheable token count (1024 tokens for most Claude models) cache_control is silently ignored — no error, billed as if caching were never requested. A single byte difference anywhere before a breakpoint (timestamp, reordered JSON keys, dynamic content mixed into the prefix) invalidates the cache for that breakpoint and everything after it, so you pay the 25% write premium with zero read discount — worse than not caching at all. Caches don't transfer across API surfaces (Anthropic Direct vs Bedrock vs Vertex are separate). Extended-thinking blocks and caching reportedly "don't mix well across providers" per ProjectDiscovery's own account.

name: Anthropic extended 1-hour cache TTL
mechanism: Same caching mechanism as above but TTL extended from the 5-minute default to 1 hour via a ttl parameter, so caches survive longer gaps between calls in agentic/long-running workflows before a full-price rewrite is forced.
savings: Anthropic restates the same "up to 90% cost / up to 85% latency" headline for the 1-hour case; no independent number isolates the TTL extension's incremental effect alone
effort: low — one parameter change
trap: The 1-hour cache write is billed at a different (higher) multiplier than the 5-minute write on Anthropic's rate card — check the current pricing page rather than assuming the same premium applies.

name: Provider caching-pricing-model divergence (Gemini vs Anthropic)
mechanism: Gemini charges $4.50/million tokens/hour as a standing fee to keep a context cache warm, billed whether or not it's read. Anthropic charges only for cache writes, and the cache's 5-minute lifetime is refreshed each time it's used — no separate storage fee.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — structural pricing-model comparison, not a percentage claim
effort: n/a — informational, changes which provider is cheaper for a given call pattern
trap: A workload with long idle gaps racks up Gemini's standing hourly fee even when the cache is never read, while the same workload on Anthropic pays one write premium and lets the cache lapse for free. Which provider is cheaper depends on calls-per-hour, not the headline discount percentage.

name: Batch API (async, 50% flat discount)
mechanism: Requests submitted as an async batch job (up to 50k requests OpenAI / 100k Anthropic), processed within a 24-hour SLA at a flat 50% discount on input+output tokens. Same model, same forward pass — only delivery timing and billing differ.
savings: flat 50% off input and output tokens, confirmed directly by both providers' own accounts
effort: low — different request/response shape but "same API shape" per one practitioner
trap: One practitioner's real measurement across ~2,800 large batch calls found practical average turnaround was 5.8 minutes, far under the notional 24-hour SLA — meaning "batch is too slow for us" is often untested folklore rather than a measured constraint for many workloads.

name: Prompt caching on a highly-repeated static prefix (video metadata case)
mechanism: Applied Anthropic prompt caching to a workload dominated by a large, repeated static prefix.
savings: $720/month → $72/month (10x, near the theoretical ~90% cache-read discount ceiling)
effort: low
trap: This 10x figure sits near the theoretical maximum, implying the workload was almost entirely repeated-prefix tokens. Most real workloads have more unique per-call content and won't hit this ceiling — treat as a best-case bound, not a typical result. Note: source is a named individual's personal blog/Medium post, not an X/Twitter thread — flagging the channel mismatch honestly.

name: OpenRouter cross-provider cache-savings audit endpoint
mechanism: OpenRouter added the ability to audit cache-read vs cache-creation token splits for OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepSeek requests routed through their proxy — an observability layer over each provider's own caching mechanism, doesn't change model behavior.
savings: N/A — tooling, not itself a savings lever
effort: low if already routing through OpenRouter
trap: Full thread content not readable (X fetch blocked in this environment) — only the announcement snippet was verified.

name: Vaudit "TokenAudit" — invoice-error recovery (not a compute technique)
mechanism: A billing-audit startup reviewed $34M in AI invoices across 60 companies (mostly Claude Code usage), March-June 2026, and claims to have found ~$1.7M in erroneous charges: billed for a newer/more expensive model than was actually used, billed for agent turns that errored/failed to complete, and "retry storms" where a failing agent's repeated retries were each billed as a full call.
providers: OpenAI (findings said to also span Amazon, Google, Microsoft)
savings: ~5% of invoiced spend recovered (1.7M/34M); ~80% of disputed line items said to be credited back after being challenged
effort: medium — requires reconciling per-request logs against per-model line-item pricing; this is literally what the vendor sells
trap: This is one level removed from primary: a vendor's own claim about their audit product's results, reported via secondary business press. I could not reach Vaudit's own primary page (403/429 on fetch) to check methodology, and no independent replication was seen. The failure modes described are structurally plausible but the headline recovery figure should be read as a sales number, not a peer-reviewed statistic, until verified.

mechanism: Undisclosed. A free-tier user with no registered payment method and zero dashboard-visible API usage received a failed-payment invoice for $1.67M, which within 24 hours became a $16.6M charge attempt. Anthropic attributed it to "a faulty auto-reload setting" without disclosing root cause, and stated it "was not the result of unauthorized access."

Individual identified only as "a Korean software developer" in press coverage (wccftech, OnMSFT, IBTimes UK, propakistani); their own original X post was not located directly via available search.
