name: Anthropic prompt caching (cache reads)
mechanism: Cache the KV-state of a repeated prompt prefix (system prompt, tool defs, long docs). A cache read is billed at 0.1x the base input-token price instead of 1x — a 90% discount on tokens that hit the cache.
savings: 90% off input-token price on cache-hit tokens (0.1x multiplier), confirmed current pricing as of fetch (Aug 2026)
effort: low (add cache_control breakpoints) to zero (Claude Code does this automatically for its own calls)
trap: Cache WRITES cost more, not less: 1.25x base price for 5-min TTL, 2x for 1-hour TTL (primary-doc). If the cached content is never re-read (one-off / non-repeated tasks), you paid a premium for zero benefit — net cost increase. HN commenter joemazerino corroborates: 'Firing off cache writing costs 1.2x tokens iirc. Meaning non repeatable tasks will cost more in the long run.' Also: raw-SDK users get zero caching unless they manually place cache_control breakpoints — several third-party 'prompt-caching' plugins exist solely to patch this gap for people building on the Anthropic SDK directly (Claude Code/Cursor/Windsurf users already get it automatically and don't need them).

name: OpenAI / Anthropic / Google Batch APIs
mechanism: Submit requests as an async batch job instead of a synchronous call; provider fills idle/off-peak GPU capacity and returns results within a 24h window.
savings: 50% off standard synchronous pricing — confirmed identically across all three providers' current primary docs (Aug 2026 fetch)
effort: medium — requires async job submission/polling instead of request/response, and tolerance for non-realtime latency
trap: HN's original 2024 batch-API launch thread (92 pts/65 comments) spent most of its energy debating why OpenAI chose polling-over-HTTP instead of a message-queue protocol — i.e., the batch API is operationally awkward (no native 'list my open jobs' endpoint at launch per commenter barbazoo) and only fits workloads that genuinely tolerate latency. OpenAI's Flex Processing (same ballpark discount, stacked with caching) trades the batch window for occasional uncharged 429 'resource unavailable' errors instead — a different but still real reliability tax.

name: Provider/route selection for an identical open-weight model (OpenRouter-style shopping)
mechanism: OpenRouter publishes 'effective pricing' / cache-hit-rate telemetry per provider per model. Providers vary enormously in whether they pass caching savings through at all.
providers: OpenRouter aggregation across DeepSeek, StepFun, Moonshot AI, Google Vertex, io.net, AkashML, SambaNova, etc.
savings: Observed real spread for the SAME model: DeepSeek V4 Pro $0.056–$1.722/M tokens (2,975% range) depending on provider; GLM-5.1 $0.323–$1.747 (440.87% range); Kimi K2.6 $0.276–$1.090 (295% range). Cache-hit rates by provider: DeepSeek 87%, StepFun 86.1%, Moonshot 84.8%, vs io.net/AkashML/SambaNova at exactly 0%. Notably Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Vertex AI shows 65.3% cache-hit vs Google's own Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview at 37.3%.
effort: low if already using an aggregator/router; requires trusting third-party infra otherwise
trap: This is a snapshot of a volatile market — the author flags hourly fluctuation. Also: 'same model' claims across re-hosted open-weight deployments are not always bit-identical (quantization, serving stack differences) even when pricing implies parity — worth flagging as an assumption to verify per-provider, not a guarantee.

name: Cache-hit-rate sensitivity of agentic bills (10:1 uncached:cached pricing ratio)
mechanism: In long agentic loops, each turn re-sends growing context. If the cache hit rate drops (context churn, cache-busting edits, TTL expiry), the fraction of tokens paying the ~10x 'uncached' price rises, compounding across turns.
providers: Generic — modeled on Anthropic/OpenAI-style 1x/10x cached:uncached ratio
savings: UNQUANTIFIED as a real production measurement — the '20% cache-hit drop doubles your bill' headline comes from a SIMULATOR, not measured logs: 'The chart below simulates the actual costs. Each turn appends 200-3000 random input tokens... a cache hit is rolled probabilistically.'
effort: n/a — this is a diagnostic, not an action
trap: Presented with simulation caveats buried below the headline; a reader skimming only the title would treat a modeled scenario as a measured fact. Good illustration of the exact kind of unsourced-adjacent claim to catch before it becomes 'data' in a sales deck.

name: MCP 'code mode' — replace per-call tool-result JSON with executable code
mechanism: Model writes/executes code that calls MCP tools directly and only returns the code's final result, instead of round-tripping full JSON tool-call/tool-result pairs through the model's context on every step.
providers: pattern also associated with Anthropic's own 'code execution with MCP' engineering post
savings: 99.2% claimed by the blog title alone — UNVERIFIED, could not fetch body (HTTP 406)
effort: unknown
trap: This is exactly the class of claim to re-fetch with a different tool/method before citing to a customer — a 99.2% headline with an inaccessible source is a red flag pattern in itself, and the '99.2%' framing directly overlaps with the 'Show HN: Callmux — MCP multiplexer that cuts tool call context pollution by ~19x' pattern also seen in this sweep, suggesting this is a known-shape claim family (tool-result JSON is genuinely often 10-50x larger than the code that would produce the same result) rather than a fabrication — but it needs a primary-source re-check before use.

name: Mid-conversation tool changes (tool_addition / tool_removal / defer_loading, beta mid-conversation-tool-changes-2026-07-01)
mechanism: The full tool set is declared once in `tools[]` up front (tools marked `defer_loading:true` are declared but withheld from the model until surfaced). Instead of editing the top-level `tools` array to add/remove a tool mid-session — which sits earliest in the cache-hash prefix (tools→system→messages) and would invalidate the ENTIRE cached conversation — you append a `{role:'system', content:[{type:'tool_addition'|'tool_removal', tool:{type:'tool_reference', name}}]}` message to `messages[]`. Because `tools[]` itself never changes bytes, the cached prefix hash is provably unaffected — CONFIRMED verbatim in the primary doc: 'The `tools` array itself never changes, so the cached prefix stays intact' and inline code comments 'earlier turns stay byte-identical and the cache still hits.'
providers: Google Vertex AI — per the live doc; NOT stated for Claude Platform on AWS or Foundry
savings: UNQUANTIFIED in $ terms, but the mechanism-level claim (cache prefix stays byte-identical) is primary-doc confirmed, not inferred.
effort: beta header + declare candidate tools with defer_loading:true + one system-message content block per add/remove
trap: This IS genuinely cache-preserving for the caching layer (Tier A claim, confirmed) — BUT it deliberately changes what tools are *offered to the model* on later turns, which is a real behavioral difference the model can act on differently (it may now call, or stop calling, a tool it couldn't/could before). So while the caching mechanism is provably identity-preserving for the cached bytes, the FEATURE'S PURPOSE is to change model capability turn-to-turn — do not conflate 'avoids cache invalidation' (true, Tier A for the cache layer) with 'output is unaffected' (false — that's not what this feature is for). Availability is also narrower than the skill's cached notes suggested for one axis: model support is Claude Fable 5, Claude Mythos 5, Opus 4.8, and Claude Opus 5 — NOT Claude Sonnet 5 (confirmed both here and for the sibling mid-conversation-system-messages feature). Tagging 'unknown' rather than A or C because the tier question as posed by the product ('does compute-reuse-only apply') doesn't cleanly map to a feature whose entire point is a mid-session capability change — settle by testing: does a session with tool_removal ever produce output a byte-identical twin session (same tools declared, none removed) would not? Almost certainly yes by design, which argues for C on the 'is output affected' axis even though the caching claim itself is A.
sources: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages (WebFetch, this session — full page fetched verbatim, includes runnable code samples in 8 languages confirming exact request/response shape)

name: Prompt cache minimum-token table + 5m/1h TTL pricing
mechanism: Pure compute-reuse: a prefix-match KV-cache. Minimum cacheable prefix length is NOT uniform across models (contrary to a naive assumption) — confirmed exact table: Claude Opus 5/Fable 5/Mythos 5 = 512 tokens; Opus 4.8/Sonnet 5/Sonnet 4.6/Sonnet 4.5/Opus 4.1/Opus 4/Sonnet 4 = 1,024; Opus 4.7/Mythos Preview/Haiku 3.5 = 2,048; Opus 4.6/Opus 4.5/Haiku 4.5 = 4,096. Pricing multipliers vs base input price: 5m-TTL write = 1.25x, 1h-TTL write = 2x, cache READ (either TTL) = 0.1x. Below the prefix minimum, a cache_control marker silently no-ops (cache_creation_input_tokens stays 0) — no error is raised.
providers: Claude API (1P), Claude Platform on AWS — confirmed automatic prompt caching NOT available on Bedrock/Vertex per shared/platform-availability.md (manual cache_control still works, but auto-caching does not); Foundry beta
savings: Cache read is 0.1x base input price (a documented, exact figure, primary-doc, both in prompt-caching.md and pricing.md, this session). name: Cache breakpoint lookback window (20 blocks) + concurrent-request cache race
mechanism: Each cache_control breakpoint walks backward at MOST 20 content blocks looking for a prior cache entry (breakpoint itself counts as position 1). If a single turn adds >20 blocks (common in tool-heavy agentic loops), the next breakpoint's lookback window will not reach the earlier cache entry and silently misses — fix is to plant an intermediate breakpoint every ~15 blocks. Separately: a cache entry only becomes readable AFTER the first response with that prefix BEGINS STREAMING — N parallel/concurrent requests sharing an identical prefix will all miss the cache and all pay full uncached price, because none of them can read what another is still in the process of writing.
providers: Claude API (1P) and anywhere prompt caching is available
savings: N/A — this is a failure-mode/edge-case description, not a savings lever itself; getting it wrong silently forfeits the cache-read discount described above.
effort: requires deliberate breakpoint placement discipline in agentic loops; for fan-out, requires sequencing the first request and awaiting its first streamed token before firing the rest
trap: Both failure modes are SILENT — no error, no warning, just cache_read_input_tokens staying at 0 or lower than expected. The concurrent-race trap is especially costly for high-QPS fan-out patterns (e.g., N parallel evaluator calls with a shared large system prompt) — naive parallel dispatch guarantees N full-price cache writes instead of 1 write + (N-1) reads.
sources: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching.md (WebFetch, this session — both the exact 20-block mechanic with worked example, and the concurrent-request section, quoted verbatim)

name: Cache-read tokens excluded from ITPM rate limits (model-specific exception: Haiku 3.5)
mechanism: For essentially all current models, `cache_read_input_tokens` do NOT count against the organization's ITPM (input-tokens-per-minute) rate limit — only `input_tokens` (post-breakpoint) and `cache_creation_input_tokens` (writes) count. This means a heavily-cached workload can process far more total input than the raw ITPM number implies (documented worked example: 2M ITPM limit + 80% cache hit rate ≈ 10M total input tokens/minute effective throughput). The ONE documented exception, marked with a dagger in the official rate-limits table: Claude Haiku 3.5 (retired except on Bedrock/Google Cloud) DOES count cache_read_input_tokens toward its ITPM.
providers: Claude API (1P) — this is the rate-limit doc's own scope; Managed Agents inherits standard ITPM/OTPM for the underlying model inference per shared/managed-agents-api-reference.md
savings: This is a rate-limit-headroom effect, not a dollar-cost effect (cache reads are ALSO separately billed at 0.1x price — the two benefits, cost reduction and rate-limit exemption, are independent and both real).
effort: N/A — automatic given caching is already in use; no separate opt-in
trap: This resolves the open question definitively for essentially every currently-relevant model EXCEPT Haiku 3.5, which is itself retired everywhere except Bedrock and Google Cloud — so in practice, on the Claude API (1P) today, the exception is close to moot, but anyone still running Haiku 3.5 traffic on Bedrock/Vertex will see cache reads eat into their rate limit unlike every other model.

name: Batch API: 50% discount, availability, and stacking with prompt-cache reads
mechanism: Message Batches API processes requests asynchronously (most complete <1hr, hard cap 24hr, results retained 29 days) at a flat 50% discount on BOTH input and output tokens vs. standard synchronous pricing, for every current model. Exact confirmed batch price table (input/output per MTok): Fable 5/Mythos 5 $5/$25, Opus 5/4.8/4.7/4.6/4.5 $2.50/$12.50, Sonnet 5 (intro) $1/$5, Sonnet 5 (from 2026-09-01)/4.6/4.5 $1.50/$7.50, Haiku 4.5 $0.50/$2.50. Availability per shared/platform-availability.md: Claude API and Claude Platform on AWS only — NOT Bedrock, NOT Vertex, NOT Foundry (❌ on all three).
savings: Exactly 50% on both input and output tokens — explicit, primary-doc, not inferred: 'All usage is charged at 50% of the standard API prices.'
effort: restructure calls as async batch requests with polling/results retrieval; no per-request code change to the model call itself beyond wrapping in a batch envelope
trap: THE REGISTER'S CLAIM THAT 'ANTHROPIC NEVER DOCUMENTS THE COMBINED RATE' IS PARTIALLY REFUTED: the STACKING itself IS explicitly documented in three independent places I fetched this session — (1) batch-processing.md: 'The pricing discounts from prompt caching and Message Batches can stack, providing even greater cost savings when both features are used together'; (2) pricing.md prompt-caching section: 'These multipliers stack with other pricing modifiers, including the Batch API discount and data residency'; (3) pricing.md FAQ: 'Batch API and prompt caching discounts can be combined. For example, using both features together provides significant cost savings.' HOWEVER — and this is the part the register may be pointing at — Anthropic does NOT publish an explicit numeric combined-rate table (e.g., no 'batched cache-read = $X/MTok' row anywhere I found). The combined rate must be INFERRED by multiplying the independently-documented multipliers: batched cache-read ≈ base_input_price × 0.1 (cache-read multiplier) × 0.5 (batch discount) = 0.05x base input price. I could not find this 0.05x figure stated anywhere verbatim — it is my inference from two documented multipliers, not a quoted number. So: the FACT of stacking is primary-doc confirmed; the EXACT combined multiplier is inferred, not documented. Cache hit rates in batches are also explicitly best-effort only (30–98% observed range depending on traffic pattern, since batch requests process concurrently and asynchronously rather than sequentially) — batch cache economics are noisier than synchronous caching. Also: fast mode is explicitly incompatible with Batch API ('Fast mode is not available with the Batch API'), and `max_tokens:0` cache pre-warming is unsupported inside a batch.

Organizations with an existing commitment can continue to use Priority Tier through their contract end date.' name: Web search and code execution: pricing, free tiers, and code-execution-is-free-when-bundled-with-search rule
mechanism: Web search: $10 per 1,000 searches flat (not per-token), PLUS standard token costs for search-generated content that enters context; each search call counts as one use regardless of result count; errored searches are NOT billed. Code execution: billed by EXECUTION TIME (not tokens) with a 5-minute MINIMUM per invocation; each org gets 1,550 FREE HOURS/MONTH; overage is $0.05/hour per container; if files are attached to a request, execution time bills even if the tool is never actually invoked (because files are preloaded onto the container). CRITICAL RULE: code execution is FREE (zero additional charge beyond token costs) whenever bundled in the same request as web_search_20260209+ or web_fetch_20260209+ — this covers BOTH the code-execution machinery behind those tools' 'dynamic filtering' AND any code Claude runs directly in that same request. Web fetch itself has NO additional charge ever — standard token costs only.
providers: Claude API (1P), Claude Platform on AWS for both tools per platform-availability.md; web search also on Foundry/Vertex(basic-only) but NOT Bedrock; code execution NOT on Bedrock/Vertex, beta on Foundry
savings: The bundling rule is a real, documented savings lever: an agent that would otherwise pay standalone code-execution container-hours can get it for free by ensuring web_search or web_fetch (v20260209+) is present in the same request — but this only applies when dynamic filtering or explicit code execution is naturally co-occurring with search/fetch, not a general-purpose way to launder unrelated code execution as free.
effort: N/A — automatic bundling rule; no special code required to get the free-when-bundled treatment beyond including both tool types in the same tools[] array (and even then it's automatic — 'the API provisions the code execution it needs for the request automatically, so you don't add the code execution tool to your request for it')
trap: The 1,550-free-hours figure is PER ORGANIZATION PER MONTH, not per API key or per request — a multi-team org sharing one workspace will exhaust the free tier faster than a naive per-project estimate assumes. The 5-minute MINIMUM per execution is easy to miss when estimating cost for many small, quick code-execution calls: 100 quick 10-second scripts still bill as 100 × 5 minutes = ~8.3 hours, not ~17 minutes.

name: Managed Agents billing: token rates, session runtime, session/deployment budgets
mechanism: Managed Agents (CMA) sessions bill on TWO independent dimensions: (1) all consumed tokens at standard per-model Messages-API rates (prompt-caching multipliers apply identically; web search still $10/1,000; fast mode premium applies if the agent's model.speed='fast'; data-residency 1.1x applies if model.inference_geo='us'), and (2) SESSION RUNTIME at a flat $0.08 per session-hour, metered to the millisecond, accruing ONLY while session.status='running' (idle/rescheduling/terminated time is free). Session runtime billing REPLACES standalone code-execution container-hour billing within CMA — no separate container charge on top. Optional SESSION BUDGETS are a hard dollar cap (`budget:{type:limit, max_list_cost:{amount, currency:USD}}`, amount in cents as an integer string) enforced as a pre-request gate before each model call — the session pauses (`stop_reason:budget_reached`, status goes idle, NOT terminated) once consumed list-cost reaches the cap; can be raised, lowered, or removed post-creation but NEVER newly added to a session created without one, and removal is one-way. DEPLOYMENT BUDGETS (scheduled/cron agents) differ: can be added on update where none existed, and cleared-then-re-added, unlike session budgets.
providers: Claude API (1P) only for Managed Agents per platform-availability.md — beta on Claude Platform on AWS, explicitly ❌ on Bedrock, Vertex, and (inferred) Foundry
savings: N/A — this is billing mechanics, not a savings technique. One EXPLICIT non-stacking finding: 'The Batch API discount does NOT apply to Managed Agents sessions' — quoted verbatim: 'Sessions are stateful and interactive. There is no batch mode.' Cloud-platform (Bedrock/Vertex) pricing also explicitly does not apply since CMA isn't available there.
effort: budget config is one object at session/deployment creation; no code beyond that to get the cost visibility (usage.list_cost reported on session object and in session.usage stream events)
trap: List-cost enforcement is a PRE-request gate, not exact — 'the request that crosses the cap completes, so the final figure can exceed the cap by at most one model request per running thread' — a budget is a soft ceiling with one-request overshoot risk, not a hard stop. Reported list_cost is rounded to the nearest cent while the actual enforcement compares exact (unrounded) amounts, meaning a session showing list_cost exactly equal to its cap may not yet be paused — you must key off `stop_reason:budget_reached`, never the displayed dollar figure, to know the session actually stopped. In multiagent sessions there is ONE shared budget across all threads (no per-thread caps), and models without a published list price can't be budgeted at all (budgeted session referencing an unpriced model returns 400). Tier tagged 'unknown' rather than A because CMA sessions run an agentic harness with server-side extended thinking ON BY DEFAULT and automatic context compaction — both of which are themselves Tier-C-affecting mechanisms bundled invisibly inside the billing wrapper; the billing layer itself is Tier A (pure metering) but the harness it meters is not behavior-neutral.

name: Token counting endpoint (/v1/messages/count_tokens): cost and rate limits
mechanism: The count_tokens endpoint is explicitly FREE TO USE ('Token counting is free to use') and has ITS OWN, SEPARATE rate-limit pool from message creation — confirmed: 'Token counting and message creation have separate and independent rate limits. Usage of one does not count against the limits of the other.' Exact RPM limits by usage tier: Start=2,000, Build=4,000, Scale=8,000 RPM. The endpoint is stateless (no caching applied to it — 'token counting provides an estimate without using caching logic. Although you may provide cache_control blocks in your token counting request, prompt caching only occurs during actual message creation'). Notable behavioral nuance for thinking-heavy workloads: thinking blocks from PREVIOUS assistant turns are excluded from the returned count, but the CURRENT turn's thinking (if you're counting a hypothetical continuation) IS included.
providers: Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry — confirmed as one of the more broadly available features, per the doc's own Compatibility section
savings: N/A — it's a free diagnostic endpoint, not a savings technique itself, but it's the correct tool for measuring the tokenizer-change savings/cost-delta described elsewhere in this research (never use tiktoken — explicitly wrong for Claude, documented to undercount by 15-20%+ on typical text).
effort: one API call per count
trap: The returned count is explicitly an ESTIMATE that 'might differ by a small amount' from actual billed tokens on the real request — and it may include 'tokens added automatically by Anthropic for system optimizations' that you are NOT billed for, meaning count_tokens can slightly OVER-report vs. actual billing in some cases. Also: server-tool token counts (web search etc.) 'only apply to the first sampling call' when counted — a multi-turn agentic tool-use estimate from this endpoint will undercount subsequent iterations.

name: Automatic prompt caching (cache reads)
mechanism: Any request ≥1,024 input tokens is automatically checked for a matching prefix from a recent request. On a hit, the reused portion is served from cached KV-state instead of being recomputed, and the customer pays the cached-input rate for that portion. No code changes, no opt-in, no separate caching product — happens on every eligible request. Matching is prefix-based: content must be byte-identical from the start of the prompt (system message, then user/assistant turns, then tools/images/schema) up to the point of divergence.
savings: Discount on the cached portion varies by model family — confirmed by diffing input vs cached-input list prices on the pricing page: gpt-4o/gpt-4o-mini = 50% off; gpt-4.1/gpt-4.1-mini/gpt-4.1-nano and o3/o4-mini = 75% off; gpt-5.6-sol/terra/luna and gpt-5.5 = 90% off. o3-mini = 50% off. This is NOT a single uniform rate — treating it as one number is a common documentation error.
effort: none — fully automatic; only effort is prompt-structuring discipline (put static content first, dynamic content last) to maximize prefix overlap
trap: On GPT-5.6+ models the write side is no longer free (see the separate cache-write-surcharge entry below) — this silently converts caching from a pure optimization into a bet. Also: caches are per-organization only, evict after inactivity (see TTL entry), and the prefix match is exact/byte-identical, so a single reordered tool definition or a timestamp inserted early in the prompt kills the entire downstream discount.

name: prompt_cache_key (cache-warm routing hint)
mechanism: An optional string parameter on Chat Completions/Responses requests. OpenAI's own text: 'Reuse the same key for those requests to help route them to the same cache.' It is billing/routing metadata only — it does not alter the prompt, the model, or the forward pass; it only influences which backend machine (and therefore which warm KV-cache) a request is dispatched to, raising the probability of a cache hit for customers with enough per-key traffic.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED as a standalone number — it doesn't create a discount itself, it raises the hit-rate for the automatic-caching discount above. OpenAI recommends keeping traffic to roughly 15 requests/minute per key to avoid the traffic fragmenting across machines and missing the cache.
effort: low — pass a stable string per logical workload/user/session
trap: It is explicitly a hint, not a guarantee ('help route') — under bursty or high-cardinality-key traffic you can pay for the discipline of setting the key and still miss the cache. It gives no visibility into hit rate beyond the per-response `cached_tokens` field, so silent degradation (e.g. traffic split across too many keys) is easy to miss without active monitoring.

name: Prompt cache TTL / retention window
mechanism: Legacy/pre-GPT-5.6 models: in-memory cache, prefixes 'generally remain active for 5 to 10 minutes of inactivity, up to a maximum of one hour'; an 'extended retention' option can hold prefixes up to 24 hours. GPT-5.6+: fixed 30-minute TTL ('the only supported value'), described as a floor ('remains eligible for reuse for at least 30 minutes, but OpenAI may retain it longer'), not a ceiling.
savings: Not a savings mechanism itself — governs the eligibility window for the read-discount above. Low-QPS workloads (per-prefix gaps longer than the TTL) get zero benefit from caching no matter how well-structured the prompt is.
effort: none for default TTL; unknown effort/cost to request extended retention on legacy models — not documented as free or as a paid add-on
trap: Extended retention's pricing is undocumented in the public guide — 'UNQUANTIFIED' whether it costs anything extra; do not assume it's free. Also, ZDR (Zero Data Retention) organizations default to in-memory-only retention for older models, which caps effective TTL well below what a non-ZDR org gets — a compliance choice with a hidden cost-optimization side effect.

name: Batch API (asynchronous 50% discount)
mechanism: Submit a JSONL file of requests; OpenAI processes them off the synchronous request path against a separate rate-limit pool and returns results typically well within 24 hours (docs: 'each batch completes within 24 hours (and often more quickly)'). Billed only for completed requests; anything not finished in the 24h window expires unbilled.
savings: 50% off both input and output token prices vs synchronous rates — stated directly on the primary docs page, applies uniformly across models (unlike the cache discount, which varies by model).
effort: medium — requires restructuring calling code to file-upload/poll/download instead of synchronous request/response, and tolerance for latency up to 24h
trap: Docs do not state, either way, whether Batch requests are served by identical model weights/precision/serving stack as the synchronous endpoint, nor whether Batch requests are themselves eligible for the prompt-caching discount on top of the 50% batch discount. I could not confirm output-distribution parity from current primary docs in this pass — tagging 'unknown' per instructions rather than assuming A. Experiment to settle it: send the same deterministic (temp=0, fixed seed where available) prompt through Batch and through Standard many times each, diff outputs/logprobs for systematic (not just sampling-noise) divergence.

name: Flex processing (service_tier=flex)
mechanism: Set `service_tier: "flex"` on Chat Completions/Responses. Docs: 'lower costs ... in exchange for slower response times and occasional resource unavailability' (429 'Resource Unavailable', explicitly unbilled when it happens). Beta, limited model availability (gpt-5.6 confirmed supported).
savings: Priced at Batch API rates (i.e. ~50% off standard) 'with additional discounts from prompt caching' stacking on top — confirmed the two discounts compound.
effort: low — one parameter — but requires raising client timeouts above the default 10 minutes and handling 429s with fallback to `service_tier: "auto"`/omitted
trap: Same unresolved parity question as Batch: no primary-doc statement confirming identical weights/precision to standard synchronous serving. Also occasional outright request failure (unbilled, but a reliability cost, not just a latency one) — not suitable for latency-sensitive or completion-critical paths.

name: Priority / Fast mode processing (service_tier=priority|fast)
mechanism: Renamed from 'Priority processing' to 'Fast mode' (per search-indexed OpenAI help-center content dated around July 30, 2026); both `service_tier: "priority"` and `service_tier: "fast"` reportedly accepted. Provides faster/more consistent latency with an enterprise SLA/SLO.
savings: This is a cost INCREASE lever, not a saving: 2× standard per-token pricing (derived/inferred from third-party pricing trackers cross-checked against the primary pricing page's flagship rate — e.g. gpt-5.6-sol Standard input $5.00 vs a reported $10.00 Fast-mode input rate). I was not able to load the primary help-center FAQ directly in this session (403 on direct fetch); this multiplier should be re-verified against `developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing?latest-pricing=priority` or the equivalent in Phase 3 before it's relied on.
effort: low — one parameter
trap: Named as a 'processing' tier, easy to mentally file next to Batch/Flex as a variant, but it is a 2x cost lever, the opposite direction from every other lever in this brief. Flag any implementation that lets `service_tier` be set upstream of a cost-optimization layer without an explicit allow-list — this is a lever that can silently double spend, not save it.

name: Scale Tier (committed throughput, pre-GPT-5.6 models)
mechanism: Enterprise-only. Purchase 'token units' (input+output tokens/minute) for a minimum 30-day commitment, scoped to one specific model snapshot. 99.9% uptime SLA, prioritized/consistent-speed compute vs pay-as-you-go. Billing detail (from search-indexed OpenAI content): if usage within a 15-minute window stays under your committed entitlement, it's not separately billed; overage is billed at standard pay-as-you-go rates.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED as a per-token discount — no primary source states Scale Tier tokens are cheaper per-token than Standard; the documented benefit is throughput/latency consistency and SLA, not a lower price. Do not sell this internally as a cost-reduction lever without a quoted rate from OpenAI sales — treat any 'Scale Tier saves X%' claim as unsourced until a contract is in hand.
effort: high — sales-gated, Enterprise-tier contract, 30-day minimum commitment, model-snapshot-locked
trap: Deprecated path forward: 'Scale Tier is available on models released before GPT-5.6. For GPT-5.6 and future model releases, see Reserved Tier' — anyone standardizing tooling on Scale Tier today is building on a track OpenAI is winding down.

name: Reserved Tier (provisioned throughput, GPT-5.6+ successor to Scale Tier)
mechanism: Enterprise-only, sales-gated. Provisioned throughput denominated in $/minute for a specific model, usable flexibly 'across Standard and Priority processing, context lengths, and regions.' In peak-load shedding scenarios, OpenAI states it will reject non-Reserved traffic before Reserved traffic — i.e. the product is priority-of-service under contention, not a discount.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — no published $/minute rate; requires contacting sales. Framed entirely around reliability/SLA, not price reduction.
effort: high — Enterprise sales contract
trap: Same as Scale Tier: don't let 'reserved capacity' get conflated with 'cheaper capacity' in the pitch deck — the primary docs never claim a per-token discount for either commitment product.

name: Predicted Outputs
mechanism: Chat Completions only (not confirmed available on Responses API or any GPT-5.x model in the current docs — supported list is gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini, gpt-4.1-nano only). You submit an expected/predicted completion; the model verifies tokens against it, reports `accepted_prediction_tokens` vs `rejected_prediction_tokens` in `usage`, and returns faster when the prediction matches. Structurally resembles speculative-decoding-style draft verification, but OpenAI's docs do not explicitly state the final output is mathematically guaranteed identical to what an unassisted generation would produce — that equivalence is assumed, not documented, so tagging 'unknown' rather than A per the brief's instruction not to default to A.
savings: NEGATIVE / cost-increase risk when predictions are wrong. Primary doc, quoted verbatim: 'any rejected tokens are still billed like other completion tokens generated by the API, so Predicted Outputs can introduce higher costs for your requests.' This is exactly the trap the brief asked to confirm: it is a latency optimization with an uncapped cost downside — a bad prediction doesn't just fail to help, it adds a full extra round of completion-token billing for every rejected token on top of the tokens for the actual correct output.
effort: medium — requires generating a plausible predicted completion (e.g. the previous version of a file being edited) and re-validating prediction quality as the task drifts
trap: The failure mode is silent and scales with how wrong the prediction is — there's no cap, no warning threshold, and no way to bound the downside per-request short of setting `max_completion_tokens` indirectly via `max_output_tokens` elsewhere. It's also incompatible with `tools` (no function calling), `n>1`, `logprobs`, `presence_penalty`/`frequency_penalty` > 0, and non-text modalities — a fairly narrow compatibility envelope that further limits where it's safe to deploy blind.

name: Structured Outputs schema compilation cache (latency, not cost)
mechanism: First request using a novel JSON schema has extra latency while OpenAI compiles/validates it; primary doc: 'subsequent requests with the same schema will not have additional latency.' This is a separate internal cache from prompt caching (which separately treats the schema as a system-message prefix and can token-cache it under the ordinary prompt-cache mechanism).
savings: UNQUANTIFIED / effectively none as a token-cost lever — docs describe only a latency benefit, not a price difference. Any token-cost saving from a stable schema comes from ordinary prompt caching (schema-as-prefix), not from this compilation cache specifically — don't double-count the two.
effort: none — automatic on schema reuse
trap: Easy to conflate with prompt caching and claim a cost benefit that the primary docs don't actually state. Keep the two mechanisms separate in the product's savings math: schema-compilation cache = latency only; schema-as-cached-prefix = the real (model-dependent 50-90%) token discount, gated on the same ≥1,024-token/TTL/exact-match rules as any other prompt cache hit.

name: Responses API previous_response_id / server-side conversation state
mechanism: Passing `previous_response_id` (or using the Conversations API) lets OpenAI reconstruct multi-turn context server-side instead of the client resending full history in the request body. Primary doc, quoted verbatim: 'Even when using previous_response_id, all previous input tokens for responses in the chain are billed as input tokens in the API.'
savings: ZERO as a standalone mechanism — explicitly documented not to reduce billed tokens vs manually resending history. Listed here (also see deadEnds) because it is a very common misconception that server-side state = cheaper multi-turn, and the brief specifically asked about it.
effort: low to use, but the token-savings expectation must be corrected
trap: The real savings on repeated multi-turn context come entirely from automatic prompt caching matching the resent prefix (turns 1..N-1 are byte-identical across turns, so they're a textbook cache hit) — NOT from conversation-state statefulness itself. On GPT-5.6+, this interacts badly with the cache-write surcharge: every turn in a growing conversation re-writes the newly-extended prefix at the 1.25× write rate before it can ever be read back, so long multi-turn conversations on GPT-5.6+ pay a compounding write tax turn over turn, partially offsetting the read-side savings from caching the earlier turns.

name: Gemini implicit context caching (Developer API & Vertex AI)
mechanism: Automatic prefix-based KV-cache reuse across requests. No customer action needed; 'enabled by default for all Gemini 2.5 and newer models' and 'in all Google Cloud projects' (Vertex). Discount applied automatically when a cache hit occurs.
providers: Google Vertex AI (branded 'Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform' docs as of Aug 2026)
savings: 90% discount on cached-portion input tokens, both surfaces. (Older doc language cites 75% for Gemini 2.0-era models; current 2.5+/3.x models are 90%.)
effort: zero — no code change; savings materialize automatically when prefixes repeat and requests with the same prefix land close together in time
trap: No SLA/guarantee — Google states there is 'no cost saving guarantee' on implicit hits (Gemini Developer API framing) even though Vertex's wording is more confident ('cost savings are automatically passed on'). Min-token floor to even be eligible: 2,048 tokens (Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash) or 4,096 tokens (Gemini 3.x/3.5/3.1 models) — short prompts never qualify. Hit rate depends on request timing/ordering that the customer doesn't fully control, so realized savings are unpredictable and cannot be sold as a fixed percentage.
sources: https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/context-cache/context-cache-overview (fetched via docs.cloud.google.com raw HTML, section 'Implicit caching')

name: Gemini explicit context caching
mechanism: Customer creates a cache entry (with TTL), pays standard input-token price to write it once, then references the cache ID on subsequent calls. Guaranteed discount when referenced, unlike implicit caching's best-effort framing.
savings: Same 90% discount on cached tokens as implicit (2.5+/3.x models; 75% on Gemini 2.0). Additional ongoing cost: storage.
effort: low — requires an explicit createCachedContent call and passing the cache ID; worth it only for content reused predictably across many calls (system prompts, long shared documents, tool schemas)
trap: Storage is billed separately and continuously for the TTL duration — Gemini Developer API prices this at $1.00 per 1M tokens per hour (Gemini 3.5 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite tiers) — so a large, rarely-hit cache can cost more in idle storage than it saves in reads. Google's Vertex page for provisioned-throughput customers states explicit caching is still 'Preview' status on Provisioned Throughput specifically (not GA) as of this writing.

name: Vertex GSU burndown discount for cached tokens under Provisioned Throughput
mechanism: When on Provisioned Throughput, cached input tokens burn down committed GSU capacity at a reduced 'burndown rate' rather than being charged in dollars. Google's own worked example for Gemini 2.5 Pro: 1 uncached input text token = 1.0 burndown unit; 1 cached input text token = 0.1 burndown unit.
savings: 90% reduction in GSU capacity consumed per cached token (matches the same 90% ratio as the dollar-denominated caching discount) — this is a capacity discount, not a direct price discount, since PT is a fixed-cost subscription regardless of tokens used.
effort: zero beyond already using explicit/implicit caching; this is an automatic side-benefit for PT customers
trap: This is a non-obvious mechanism: caching does NOT reduce your PT dollar bill (PT is a fixed subscription) — it only frees up headroom under your already-purchased GSU ceiling, letting the same commitment serve more traffic. A team evaluating 'will caching save us money on PT' needs to reframe the question as 'will caching let us buy fewer GSUs.'

name: Vertex AI Provisioned Throughput (GSU) — committed capacity vs on-demand break-even
mechanism: GSU (Generative AI Scale Unit) is a fixed-term (1-week/1-month/3-month/1-year), fixed-cost subscription for dedicated throughput, priced per GSU per commitment period. Real published table (Google Cloud, checked 2026-08): 1-week $1,200/GSU (Global) or $1,320 (non-Global); 1-month $2,700; 3-month $2,400/mo; 1-year $2,000/mo. Longer terms compound the discount (1-year is 26% cheaper per-GSU-month than 1-month).
savings: INFERRED, and the answer is uncomfortable for the 'committed capacity always wins' narrative: using Google's own worked example (Gemini 2.0 Flash, 10 QPS sustained, mixed text/audio/output query, needing 17 GSUs), the 1-year committed cost is $34,000/month. Recomputing the identical traffic against Gemini 2.0 Flash's own published on-demand token pricing ($0.15/1M text-in, $1.00/1M audio-in, $0.60/1M text-out) gives ≈$21,500/month on-demand for the SAME sustained, 100%-utilized workload. Every commitment tier (1-week through 1-year) prices ABOVE on-demand for this workload — PT is 58% more expensive than on-demand even at full utilization for this model/traffic mix.
effort: high to evaluate correctly — requires per-model burndown-rate math (Google publishes a burndown-rate table per model/modality), not just a token-count comparison; most back-of-envelope comparisons will get this wrong
trap: THE central trap for this deal-desk question: provisioned/committed capacity is routinely sold and assumed as a cost-saving lever. On Vertex, for at least this real published example, it is NOT — GSU pricing did not beat on-demand at any commitment length, even at the exact utilization the customer sized it for. GSU's value proposition is request prioritization, deterministic monthly billing, and consistent latency — not unit-price savings — unless the specific model/modality mix has burndown ratios that diverge favorably from its on-demand price ratios (untested here for Pro-tier models; would need the same derivation repeated per model before generalizing). Do not assume this generalizes to Gemini 2.5/3.x Pro-tier models without redoing the calculation — burndown rates and on-demand prices are published per-model and the relationship could differ.
sources: https://cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/generative-ai/pricing (raw HTML: GSU price table + worked example calculation)
https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing (Gemini 2.0 Flash on-demand pricing used for the comparison)

name: Gemini Batch API / Vertex Batch prediction
mechanism: Submit prompts for async processing (results within a job window rather than real-time), letting Google batch/schedule GPU work more efficiently.
savings: Flat 50% off both input and output token price, confirmed across Gemini 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite, 2.5 Pro, 2.5 Flash, 2.5 Flash-Lite, 2.0 Flash in the current pricing page.
effort: medium — requires restructuring the calling pattern to async/job-based; only viable for workloads that tolerate non-real-time turnaround
trap: Not documented as stackable with context caching in the same request in the primary docs reviewed (unlike Anthropic direct API, which explicitly supports cache+batch together) — could not confirm or deny stacking from primary sources in the time available; treat as unverified, do not assume compounding discounts.

name: AWS Bedrock prompt caching
mechanism: Customer places 'cache checkpoints' (cachePoint / cache_control) after static prefix content (system prompt, tools, documents). Supported via Converse, ConverseStream, InvokeModel, InvokeModelWithResponseStream, and Prompt Management. Claude models on Bedrock also get 'simplified cache management' — a single trailing checkpoint that auto-scans back ~20 content blocks for the best matching prefix.
providers: AWS Bedrock — Anthropic Claude (all current 4.x models), Amazon Nova (all, automatic), OpenAI GPT-5.6 family (explicit breakpoints) and pre-5.6 (automatic)
savings: Verified with real Bedrock billing meter data (US East N. Virginia, Aug 2026): for Claude Sonnet 4.5/4.6, standard input $3.00/1M, cache read $0.30/1M (exactly 90% discount), 5-min cache write $3.75/1M (1.25x input), 1-hour cache write $6.00/1M (2x input). Claude Opus 4.5/4.6: input $5.00, cache read $0.50 (90% off), writes $6.25/$10.00. Claude Haiku 4.5: input $1.00, cache read $0.10 (90% off). These ratios are IDENTICAL to Anthropic's own direct-API cache pricing structure.
effort: low-medium — place cache breakpoints in system/tools/messages after static content; minimum checkpoint size varies by model (4,096 tokens for Opus 4.5/4.6, Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5; 1,024 tokens for Sonnet 4.6, Claude 3.5/3.7, and OpenAI models on Bedrock)
trap: 1) Prompt caching is EXPLICITLY NOT SUPPORTED with the batch inference API on Bedrock — you cannot stack the 50% batch discount with the ~90% cache-read discount on Bedrock (unlike some competing claims for Azure). 2) TTL is short (5 min default; 1 hour available on Opus 4.5/4.6, Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5 only, not Sonnet 4.6) and resets on each hit, not extends — a quiet workload will silently fall back to full price. 3) Cache checkpoints are processed tools→system→messages in a fixed chain; editing an earlier section (e.g. tools) invalidates every checkpoint after it, a common accidental-cache-buster in agent loops that regenerate tool schemas per call.
sources: AWS Bedrock retail pricing JSON, live-fetched: https://b0.p.awsstatic.com/pricing/2.0/meteredUnitMaps/bedrockfoundationmodels/USD/current/bedrockfoundationmodels.json (cross-referenced against token IDs embedded in https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/)

name: AWS Bedrock batch inference — and the 'Bedrock lacks Anthropic Batch API' claim
mechanism: Submit JSONL requests via S3, processed asynchronously, results delivered to an output S3 bucket.
providers: AWS Bedrock — Anthropic Claude (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku, current and prior generations), Amazon Nova, DeepSeek, Meta Llama, Mistral, and others
savings: 50% off on-demand, confirmed with real billing data: Claude Sonnet 4.5/4.6 batch input $1.50/1M (vs $3.00 on-demand), batch output $7.50/1M (vs $15.00); Claude Opus 4.5/4.6 batch $2.50/$12.50 (vs $5.00/$25.00); Claude Haiku 4.5 batch $0.50/$2.50 (vs $1.00/$5.00).
effort: medium — requires the S3-based batch job workflow rather than a direct synchronous call
trap: VERIFIED FALSE / DEBUNKED: the register's claim that 'Bedrock lacks the Anthropic Batch API' does not hold up. Bedrock's batch-inference support table explicitly lists Claude 3 Haiku/Opus/Sonnet through Claude Opus 4.5/4.6, Haiku 4.5, and Sonnet 4/4.5/4.6 as batch-inference-capable across many regions, and the live pricing meter data returns real (non-N/A) batch prices for all current-generation Claude models. The actual gaps between Bedrock and the native Anthropic API are elsewhere — no Claude Managed Agents, no native code execution, no native web search/fetch tool, and Anthropic Console features (prompt improvement, evaluations) don't exist on Bedrock; new model/feature releases also land on Bedrock with a lag versus the direct API. Also note: batch inference does NOT support tool calling or structured output (response_format) on Bedrock — each record is processed independently with no multi-turn capability, which silently breaks tool-using batch workloads.
sources: AWS Bedrock retail pricing JSON (live-fetched, see previous entry)

name: AWS Bedrock Provisioned Throughput (Reserved Tier) — committed capacity vs on-demand break-even
mechanism: For Anthropic Claude models specifically, Bedrock publishes a self-serve 'Reserved Tier' priced per hour per 1,000 Input-TPM and per 1,000 Output-TPM, with 1-month and 3-month commitment options. (Note: this is DIFFERENT from the generic 'Model Units' provisioned-throughput mechanism used by most other Bedrock model providers, which is NOT self-serve-priced — AWS's own docs say to 'contact your AWS account manager' for MU pricing on those. Claude gets its own transparent, published reserved-tier pricing.)
providers: AWS Bedrock — Anthropic Claude only (Opus 4.5/4.6, Sonnet 4.5/4.6, Haiku 4.5 confirmed)
savings: PRECISELY QUANTIFIED from live billing data, cross-checked against on-demand pricing: Claude Sonnet 4.5/4.6 1-month reserved tier = $0.18/hr per 1K input-TPM and $0.90/hr per 1K output-TPM. On-demand equivalent for the same sustained throughput (1,000 tokens/min for 60 min = 60,000 tokens at $3.00/$15.00 per 1M) = exactly $0.18 and $0.90. THE 1-MONTH COMMITMENT IS PRICED AT EXACT ON-DEMAND PARITY AT 100% UTILIZATION — 0% discount. The 3-month commitment is $0.162/$0.81 — a flat 10% discount at any utilization, i.e. break-even utilization for the 3-month term is 90%. Identical ratio verified independently for Opus 4.5/4.6 ($0.30/$1.50 → $0.27/$1.35, still exactly matching on-demand $5/$25 and a 10% 3-month discount) and Haiku 4.5 ($0.06/$0.30 → $0.054/$0.27, matching on-demand $1/$5).
effort: high to evaluate correctly, trivial once the ratio is known — the math is 'is my sustained utilization ≥90%'
trap: THIS IS THE SHARPEST FINDING IN THE WHOLE REGISTER for the committed-capacity question. On Bedrock, committing to Claude Provisioned Throughput for 1 month provides ZERO unit-price discount vs plain pay-per-token — you are paying exactly what on-demand would cost AT THE EXACT THROUGHPUT YOU SIZED FOR, and strictly more if actual usage comes in under that ceiling (which it almost always will, since traffic is bursty and TPM is a peak-capacity reservation, not an average). The only discount available is the 3-month term's flat 10% — and even that requires ~90% sustained utilization of the committed TPM to actually realize 10% net savings; below that, you're paying a premium for the SLA/priority/rate-limit-avoidance, not for a lower unit price. Sell PT on Bedrock as a latency/rate-limit/availability lever, never as a cost-savings lever, unless the customer's sustained utilization is verifiably ≥90% and they commit for 3 months.
sources: AWS Bedrock pricing page raw HTML, 'Reserved Tier Pricing' table for Anthropic: https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/
AWS Bedrock retail pricing JSON (live-fetched meteredUnitMaps endpoint, same as above)

name: AWS Bedrock cross-region inference (Geo vs Global)
mechanism: Geographic cross-region inference profiles route within a geography (e.g. all US regions) at the same price as single-region. A separate 'Global' cross-region inference profile routes across all AWS regions worldwide and is priced lower.
providers: AWS Bedrock — Anthropic Claude (Global cross-region profile confirmed for Sonnet 4.5)
savings: Verified with real billing data: Claude Sonnet 4.5 Global cross-region = $3.00/1M input, $15.00/1M output. Geo/in-region cross-region = $3.30/1M input, $16.50/1M output. Global is exactly 10% cheaper than Geo/in-region for identical output tokens.
effort: zero — pick the `global.` vs geography-prefixed (`us.`, `apac.`, etc.) inference-profile ID at call time; purely a routing/config choice
trap: Global routing means the request can be served from any AWS region worldwide, which has data-residency implications many enterprise customers will reject regardless of the 10% discount — this lever is unusable for regulated/data-residency-constrained customers, so don't lead with it in an enterprise pitch without first confirming residency isn't a blocker.
sources: AWS Bedrock pricing page raw HTML, 'Global Cross-region Inference' and 'Geo and In-region Cross-region Inference' tables, cross-referenced against retail pricing JSON

name: AWS Bedrock Marketplace private offers / enterprise custom pricing
mechanism: AWS Marketplace sellers (including some model providers) can issue private offers — custom pricing/EULA/payment terms visible only to one customer account. Separately, and more relevant to flagship Claude/Titan/Nova pricing specifically, enterprise-wide volume discounts are typically negotiated via AWS's standard Enterprise Discount Program (EDP) / Private Pricing Agreements at the account level, not via the Bedrock Marketplace private-offer mechanism.
providers: AWS account-level EDP/Private Pricing Agreement (covers all Bedrock spend including first-party models)
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — negotiated case-by-case, not published. No primary-doc percentage found.
effort: high — requires an AWS account team relationship and typically a committed annual spend threshold to be worth negotiating
trap: Easy to conflate 'Bedrock Marketplace private offers' (a mechanism for buying specific third-party/niche models with custom terms) with 'we can get a discount on Claude via Bedrock' — the flagship Anthropic models on Bedrock are NOT typically sold through the Marketplace private-offer mechanism; enterprise discounting on those goes through the account-level EDP instead. Don't pitch 'Marketplace private offer' language to a customer asking about discounted Claude access on Bedrock — it's the wrong mechanism name and may confuse their procurement team.

name: Azure OpenAI Provisioned Throughput (PTU) — hourly vs monthly vs annual reservation break-even
mechanism: Three deployment scopes — Global Provisioned, Data Zone Provisioned (US/EU), Regional Provisioned — each billed either hourly (no commitment, cancel anytime) or via an Azure Reservation (1-month or 1-year prepaid/committed term) for a discounted effective $/PTU rate.
savings: PRECISELY QUANTIFIED — pulled live from Microsoft's own public Azure Retail Prices API (prices.azure.com, not a scraped blog number): Global tier — hourly PAYG $1.00/PTU-hr ($730/mo equivalent if run 24/7); 1-month reservation $260/PTU-month; 1-year reservation $2,652/PTU-year ($221/mo equivalent). Data Zone — hourly $1.10/PTU-hr; 1-month reservation $286; 1-year $2,916/yr ($243/mo). Regional — hourly $2.00/PTU-hr (2x Global); 1-month reservation $286 (SAME as Data Zone); 1-year $2,916/yr (same as Data Zone). BREAK-EVEN UTILIZATION for the 1-month reservation to beat hourly billing: Global/Data Zone need the deployment running >~260 hours/month (~36% of a 730-hour month); Regional needs only >143 hours/month (~20%) because Regional's hourly PAYG rate is disproportionately high relative to its reservation price. 1-year reservations beat 1-month reservations by an additional ~15% (Global/Data Zone) at any utilization once you're committing at all.
effort: medium — sizing requires Microsoft's PTU capacity calculator (traffic shape → normalized TPM → PTU count) since throughput-per-PTU varies by model and by cache hit rate
trap: 1) A large fraction of '2026 Azure OpenAI pricing guide' blog posts scrape the un-rendered HTML shell of the public Azure pricing page, which contains numerically real (not placeholder) values because PTU pricing genuinely IS model-agnostic and identical across every model row on that page — don't assume a repeated number across all models is a scraping bug; verify against the Retail Prices API before either trusting or dismissing it. 2) Regional PTU deployments require a much higher minimum purchase (50 PTUs) than Global or Data Zone (15 PTUs) — the cheapest-to-justify tier (Regional, ~20% break-even) also has the highest capital-commitment floor. 3) Capacity is NOT guaranteed by having quota — Microsoft explicitly warns deployments can fail even with approved quota if regional capacity is exhausted, and deleting/scaling down releases capacity with no guarantee of getting it back.
sources: Azure Retail Prices API, live-queried: https://prices.azure.com/api/retail/prices (serviceName='Foundry Models', productName='Azure AI Foundry Provisioned Throughput Reservation' and 'Azure OpenAI' Provisioned Managed Global/DataZone/Regional Unit meters) — this is Microsoft's own machine-readable billing meter data, unambiguously primary

name: Azure OpenAI Batch API
mechanism: Submit jobs for processing within a 24-hour window at a discounted 'Global Standard' batch rate.
savings: 50% off Global Standard on-demand pricing, confirmed via live Retail Prices API data (e.g., GPT-5.2 Global batch input $0.875/1M vs on-demand — consistent 50% ratio pattern across the GPT-5 family checked).
effort: medium — async job submission workflow
trap: Batch and cache discounts DO appear to stack on Azure (found real distinct meters like '5.4 Batch cd inp Gl' priced below both the plain-batch and plain-cached rates individually) — unlike Bedrock, where caching is explicitly disallowed on batch. This wasn't confirmed against prose documentation (only inferred from meter existence/pricing), so treat the stacking behavior as 'observed in billing data, not confirmed in writing' — verify with a live test before promising a customer the compounded rate.
sources: Azure Retail Prices API, live-queried (productName contains 'GPT5', meterName contains 'Batch')

name: Azure OpenAI prompt caching
mechanism: Automatic for all models GPT-4o and newer once prompt exceeds 1,024 tokens with an identical first-1,024-token prefix; cache hits occur every additional 128 identical tokens thereafter. GPT-5.6+ models add explicit cache breakpoints (`prompt_cache_breakpoint`) and a `prompt_cache_key` for improved hit-matching, plus a cache-write charge that didn't exist pre-5.6.
providers: Azure OpenAI / Microsoft Foundry Models, Standard (pay-as-you-go) deployments
savings: Discount rate confirmed at exactly 90% for the GPT-5 tier via live billing data (GPT-5 Global: standard input $2.50/1M, cached input $0.25/1M = 10% of standard). Secondary/blog sources claim 25% of standard for GPT-4.1/o4-mini and 50% of standard for GPT-4o — these ratios were NOT independently re-verified against the Retail Prices API in this pass (session time-boxed); treat as practitioner-level confidence, not primary-doc confidence, until re-checked.
effort: zero for automatic caching (pre-5.6 models); low for explicit breakpoints (5.6+) — place a breakpoint after stable content
trap: 1) On Provisioned Throughput (PTU-M) deployments, cached tokens get up to a 100% discount (they don't consume PTU capacity at all, per Microsoft's docs) — a STRONGER cache benefit than Standard deployments' ~90% dollar discount, and notably stronger than Vertex's PT-caching interaction (which only gives a 90% capacity discount, not 100%). 2) PTU-M deployments do NOT support prompt cache breakpoints or expose `cache_write_tokens` — caching still works but you lose fine-grained control on Provisioned deployments. 3) A single character difference anywhere in the first 1,024 tokens causes a full cache miss (`cached_tokens`=0) — no partial credit. 4) On GPT-5.6+, if a `prompt_cache_key` gets more than ~15 requests/minute, some requests miss the cache even with an identical prefix — high-QPS single-tenant workloads need to shard across multiple cache keys to sustain hit rate.
sources: Azure Retail Prices API, live-queried (GPT5 cached-input meters)

name: Azure OpenAI Data Zone vs Global vs Regional deployment pricing
mechanism: Three deployment scopes trade data-residency guarantees for price: Global (routes anywhere), Data Zone (stays within US or EU geographic zone), Regional (stays in one specific Azure region).
savings: Confirmed EXACTLY 10% Data Zone premium over Global via live billing data for the entire GPT-5 family checked (GPT-5: Global input $2.50/1M vs Data Zone $2.75/1M; Global output $20.00 vs Data Zone $22.00 — same 10% ratio holds for GPT-5-mini, GPT-5.1-codex, and others sampled). This is a standard-deployment (pay-as-you-go) finding; PTU reservation pricing showed the SAME 10% Data Zone premium independently (Global $260/mo vs Data Zone $286/mo — 286/260=1.10).
effort: zero — pure deployment-type choice at provisioning time, no code change
trap: Regional deployments are NOT simply 'Data Zone but narrower' pricing-wise for Standard/pay-as-you-go — Regional PTU hourly pricing is 2x Global ($2.00 vs $1.00/hr) even though Regional's RESERVATION price matches Data Zone exactly. A customer choosing Regional for residency reasons and staying on hourly billing pays double Global's PTU rate; the same customer committing to even a 1-month reservation pays no premium over Data Zone. This makes 'stay on hourly PTU billing while regionally constrained' an unusually expensive choice specifically on Azure.
sources: Azure Retail Prices API, live-queried across multiple model families and deployment-scope meter names

name: Azure OpenAI PTU spillover
mechanism: When a PTU deployment returns non-200 (e.g. 429, capacity exhausted), spillover automatically redirects the overflow request to a paired standard pay-as-you-go deployment in the same resource, rather than failing the request. Configurable resource-wide or per-request via the `x-ms-spillover-deployment` header.
providers: Azure OpenAI / Microsoft Foundry Models — all Azure OpenAI models that support Provisioned Throughput
savings: N/A directly (this is an availability lever, not a discount) — but it prevents the alternative cost of failed requests / dropped traffic during bursts, and lets a customer safely under-provision PTU capacity for peak load rather than over-buying to cover tail bursts.
effort: low — a deployment-config toggle
trap: Only Azure OpenAI models support spillover — Foundry Models from other providers hosted on the same platform (Azure DeepSeek, Meta Llama) do NOT support it as of the current docs. A multi-model deployment strategy that assumes uniform spillover behavior across all Foundry models will silently fail for non-OpenAI models during a burst.

name: AWS Bedrock Provisioned Throughput for non-Anthropic models (generic Model Units)
mechanism: Model Units (MUs) define a fixed input/output token-per-minute throughput level per model, purchased with no-commitment, 1-month, or 6-month terms; the longer the term, the deeper the hourly discount.
providers: AWS Bedrock — all non-Anthropic providers (Amazon, Meta, Mistral, Cohere, etc.) and Anthropic models when using the older generic PT mechanism rather than the Claude-specific Reserved Tier
savings: UNQUANTIFIED from primary docs for current-generation models — AWS's own documentation states 'for pricing per MU... contact your AWS account manager' for most models. A single concrete example survives in AWS's own docs (a Cohere custom fine-tuned model): $39.60/month for a 1-month-commitment provisioned throughput unit, alongside secondary/blog figures for Meta Llama 2 13B (~$21/hr no-commit, ~$13/hr at 6-month commit) which could not be re-verified against a live pricing feed in this session.
effort: high — requires direct AWS account-team engagement to get a quote at all
trap: This opacity is itself the finding: unlike Google (fully published GSU table) and Microsoft (fully published PTU reservation pricing via a public API) and even AWS's own Claude Reserved Tier (published), AWS deliberately does NOT publish self-serve provisioned-throughput pricing for the bulk of its model catalog. A prospect asking 'what does Bedrock PT cost for model X' outside of Claude cannot get a self-serve answer — this is a real competitive/procurement-friction difference worth flagging, not a gap in this research.

name: Vertex AI vs Gemini Developer API — context caching parity
mechanism: Both surfaces implement the same two-tier caching model (automatic implicit + manual explicit) with the same discount math.
savings: Confirmed near-identical: both give 90% off cached tokens (2.5+/3.x models), both have no storage cost for implicit caching, both charge storage only for explicit caching. The one documented wording difference: Gemini Developer API frames implicit-cache savings as best-effort ('no cost saving guarantee'), while Vertex/Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform docs state savings are 'automatically passed on' with more confident phrasing — functionally the mechanism is identical, so this reads as a documentation-tone difference rather than a real behavioral one.
effort: n/a — informational, for choosing/positioning between surfaces
trap: Google's branding has shifted mid-2026 — the enterprise surface is now documented under 'Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform' rather than the older 'Vertex AI Generative AI' docs tree, and cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/... URLs increasingly 301-redirect into that new doc tree. Anyone hard-linking old Vertex AI caching/PT doc URLs in internal materials should expect link rot and re-verify before citing.

name: Anthropic Enterprise/Custom committed-spend discount
mechanism: Commit to a $ spend floor per month/year in exchange for a discounted per-token rate; Start/Build/Scale tiers have fixed $500/$1,000/$200,000 monthly caps, Custom tier is uncapped and individually negotiated with an account team.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED against any primary Anthropic source. Secondary SEO sites claim 10-40% scaling by commit size — treat as noise, not a finding.
effort: Low-medium: sales conversation once spend clears an unstated threshold; Custom tier requires an account team relationship
trap: Commit dollars are typically use-it-or-lose-it; under-consumption forfeits committed spend at term end. No public rollover/overage terms exist to verify against in negotiation.

name: OpenAI Enterprise committed-spend / volume discount
mechanism: Annual committed spend (paid upfront or quarterly) unlocks OpenAI's full enterprise rate schedule and access to Scale Tier/Priority Processing/Reserved Capacity purchasing mechanisms.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — openai.com/business/pricing returned 403 to WebFetch every attempt this session, so no primary confirmation of any percentage was obtained. Secondary sites claim 15-40% at $250K-$5M commits; unverified.
effort: Low-medium: requires an annual prepay commitment as a prerequisite
trap: Every specific discount number found for OpenAI Enterprise this session traces to SEO/aggregator content, not openai.com itself — do not quote these numbers to a counterparty as if verified.

name: Azure OpenAI Provisioned Throughput Units (PTU) + Azure Reservations
mechanism: PTU deployments are billed hourly ($/PTU/hr) regardless of tokens consumed. Azure Reservations are a separate financial discount applied to that hourly meter for a 1-month or 1-year commitment. Reservations and deployments are purchased independently — you must confirm deployable capacity exists BEFORE buying the reservation.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED with primary confirmation — Microsoft's own concept doc does not state a percentage. Secondary sources claim up to 70-85% vs hourly for annual reservations and cite break-even at 80-91% sustained utilization; unverified against a primary number.
effort: Medium: requires PTU sizing (RPM, token volumes, output/input ratio, cache rate) via Microsoft's capacity calculator before committing
trap: 'Reservations don't guarantee capacity' — capacity is finite and dynamically allocated; you can prepay for a reservation and still be unable to deploy the PTUs in your region. Also model-independent PTU quota is region- and deployment-type-scoped and does not transfer.

name: Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput (model units, 1-month/6-month commit)
mechanism: Purchase dedicated 'model units' at an hourly rate guaranteeing tokens/minute throughput instead of pay-per-request; commitment terms are no-commitment, 1-month, or 6-month.
providers: AWS Bedrock (hosts Anthropic Claude, Meta Llama, Cohere, others)
savings: Confirmed for Meta Llama 2 on aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing: 1-month $21.18/hr vs 6-month $13.08/hr per model unit (~38% reduction). Claude-specific PT pricing is explicitly NOT published — 'reach out to your account team.'
effort: Medium: requires demand forecasting; fixed hourly cost regardless of actual utilization
trap: Because Claude PT pricing is unpublished, there is no way to comparison-shop or sanity-check the account team's quote before committing — asymmetric information favors AWS/Anthropic in this specific negotiation.

name: AWS Marketplace private offer drawing down existing EDP/PPA commitment
mechanism: Buy an AWS-Marketplace-listed AI SaaS product (including Claude Enterprise / Bedrock-hosted models) via a negotiated private offer; the invoice counts against (retires) an already-owed AWS Enterprise Discount Program / Private Pricing Agreement commitment rather than requiring new incremental budget.
savings: Not a unit-price discount — converts otherwise-forfeited committed dollars into paid-for LLM usage, effectively up to 100% of the applied spend. Multiple independent secondary sources converge on a 'commonly up to 25% of EDP/PPA commitment' ceiling for Marketplace drawdown, but I could not find this percentage stated in an AWS primary document this session.
effort: Medium-high: requires an existing large-EDP relationship, a negotiated private offer, and procurement sign-off to route spend through Marketplace instead of direct vendor billing
trap: MAJOR, dated: as of May 1, 2025 AWS restricted eligibility to SaaS products 'fully deployed on AWS infrastructure' — hybrid/multi-cloud products no longer qualify for commitment retirement. This mechanism cleanly works for AWS-native listings (Bedrock/Claude) but NOT for a reseller product wrapping an Azure-hosted OpenAI API.

name: Google Cloud Marketplace private offer (MCPO) drawing down committed spend
mechanism: Same logic as the AWS mechanism — a negotiated Marketplace Channel Private Offer draws down an existing Google Cloud spend commitment.
savings: Secondary source claims '100% commit drawdown tied to final negotiated private-offer price, capped at 25% of total commitment,' effective June 9, 2025. Single-sourced, not verified against a Google primary doc (search budget exhausted before I could fetch cloud.google.com's own pages).
effort: Medium-high, same as AWS variant
trap: Whether Google applies an AWS-style 'fully deployed on GCP' eligibility restriction is unknown — an open question, not confirmed either way.

name: Azure MACC drawdown via native Azure OpenAI Service (no marketplace step needed)
mechanism: Because Azure OpenAI Service is a first-party Azure service rather than a third-party Marketplace listing, it may draw down a Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment (MACC) directly and automatically, without a private-offer step at all.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — not verified this session.
effort: n/a until confirmed
trap: Some specialized/PaaS Azure SKUs are historically excluded from MACC eligibility lists; do not assume Azure OpenAI Service qualifies without checking Microsoft's current official MACC-eligible-services documentation.

name: Anthropic's own Claude Marketplace commit drawdown for partner solutions
mechanism: Distinct from cloud-EDP mechanisms — organizations with an existing Anthropic spend commitment can redirect 'some of it' to pay for Claude-powered partner/ISV products; Anthropic manages the invoicing centrally.
savings: No percentage cap stated on the primary page fetched; mechanism exists but is unquantified.
effort: Requires contacting an Anthropic account team to activate
trap: The page explicitly does not quantify what fraction of the commitment is eligible ('apply some of it') — must be negotiated case by case, and it's unclear whether this interacts with or duplicates the AWS/GCP marketplace drawdown routes when buying Claude through those clouds instead.

name: Anthropic Startup Program credits
mechanism: Direct application; awardees may receive API credits, priority rate limits, and/or resource access at Anthropic's sole discretion. No dollar figure is stated in the official terms.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED against the primary source. Secondary deal-aggregator sites claim up to $25K direct track / up to $100K combined across VC-partner and Menlo-Ventures Anthology-fund tiers — unverified.
effort: Low: application-based
trap: Sanctioned-country exclusions apply (Belarus, China, Cuba, Iran, Myanmar, North Korea, Russia, Sudan, Syria, Crimea/DPR/LPR); award is entirely at Anthropic's discretion with no guarantee; targeted at early-stage startups, not applicable to an established enterprise's procurement strategy.

name: Hyperscaler startup cloud-credit programs (AWS Activate / Google for Startups / Azure Founders Hub)
mechanism: Free/discounted cloud credits usable partly against LLM API spend if the model is hosted on that cloud (Bedrock, Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI).
savings: UNQUANTIFIED against any of the three providers' own program pages — none fetched successfully this session (search budget exhausted first). Secondary aggregator sites claim AWS Activate $1K (self-serve) to $5K-$100K (VC-referred); Google Start tier $2K, Scale tier up to $100K Y1 + $100K Y2, AI-First up to $350K total; Azure Founders Hub up to $150K over 4 years.
effort: Low-medium depending on tier (self-serve vs VC/accelerator referral for larger amounts)
trap: Credits typically apply to general cloud consumption on that specific cloud, not to a direct API bill from a provider not natively hosted there — e.g. Azure credits don't offset a direct openai.com API invoice, only Azure OpenAI Service usage.

name: Anthropic Claude for Nonprofits (sector discount)
mechanism: Sector discount program launched with GivingTuesday; includes discounted Team/Enterprise seats plus free 'AI Fluency for Nonprofits' training and implementation partners (Bridgespan, Idealist Consulting, Vera Solutions, Slalom).
savings: Trade-press reporting (syndicating Anthropic's own announcement) states 'up to 75% discount on Team and Enterprise plans.' Not independently fetched from anthropic.com this session.
effort: Low: apply with nonprofit status verification
trap: Discount is described as applying to seat-based Team/Enterprise plans — unclear whether API/token pricing gets any equivalent discount; not confirmed.

name: OpenAI for Nonprofits + Researcher Access Program
mechanism: (a) Discounted ChatGPT Business/Enterprise seats for verified nonprofits; (b) Researcher Access Program grants API credits to individuals with active academic/research-org affiliation.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED against a primary source — every help.openai.com page attempted this session (Researcher Access FAQ, Nonprofits article) returned 403. Secondary snippets claim ChatGPT Business nonprofit rate ~$8-10/user/mo (vs ~$25-30 standard), $1,000 in Researcher Access API credits valid 12 months, and a separate $2,500 baseline credit via a GitLab Foundation/OpenAI fund.
effort: Low: application-based
trap: Secondary sources state the nonprofit discount explicitly does NOT extend to direct API pricing — it's a separate, smaller, capped program. None of this was verified against OpenAI's own pages this session.

name: Volume-tier negotiation benchmark claims (cross-provider) — flagged as noise cluster
mechanism: Enterprise buyers negotiate off list rate using commit size, contract duration, overage-rate caps, and unused-commit rollover as levers.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED / NOISE — a cluster of SEO sites (redresscompliance.com, thenegotiationexperts.com, vendorbenchmark.com, atonementlicensing.com, spendhound.com, morphllm.com, npifinancial.com, claude-api-cookbook.vercel.app) publish near-identical, suspiciously precise commit-tier percentage bands (e.g. '$250K-$1M → 10-15% off; $1M-$5M → 15-25%; $5M+ → 25-40%') with no named source or visible methodology. None of the providers publish this. Reported here ONLY to flag it as noise.
effort: n/a
trap: Anchoring a real negotiation on these fabricated-looking benchmark numbers is itself the risk — a procurement team could walk in mis-anchored in either direction.

name: Priority/Scale tiers as capacity levers (commonly mis-bought as 'savings')
mechanism: OpenAI Scale Tier (committed throughput ≥30 days, reserved capacity, reported 99.9% SLA), OpenAI/Azure Priority Processing (per-token premium for guaranteed latency, no long-term commitment needed per Azure's own comparison table), Anthropic Priority Tier (confirmed via dedicated 'anthropic-priority-input/output-tokens-*' response headers in the primary rate-limits doc).
savings: NEGATIVE — these are cost-increase levers, catalogued because FinOps teams routinely over-buy priority/guaranteed-latency capacity for workloads that don't need it, inflating spend without any output change.
effort: n/a
trap: Azure's own deployment-type table explicitly distinguishes Priority Processing (pay-per-token at a priority rate, no commitment) from Provisioned/PTU (dedicated capacity, commitment-based) — conflating the two when budgeting leads to paying for a guarantee you didn't need.

name: Waste pattern: forgotten nightly evals/cron jobs on paid API keys
mechanism: Eval suites or scheduled agent jobs set up during a project and never decommissioned keep billing against production API keys indefinitely. The fix (killing the job or capping its key's budget) doesn't touch any model's behavior, it just stops paying for unread output.
savings: UNQUANTIFIED — no specific case study found this session; pattern-matched from general FinOps-for-AI commentary rather than a named incident.
effort: Low once found, but discovery is the hard part without per-key cost attribution already in place
trap: Invisible in a total-spend dashboard until someone manually audits API keys against active projects — this is precisely why tagging/attribution (next item) is a prerequisite, not optional.

name: Tagging/attribution layer for showback → chargeback
mechanism: Providers do not natively expose team/cost-center/environment in billing (invoices show spend by API key or project only). FinOps Foundation guidance: (a) provision API keys with a captured requesting-team/app/cost-center at issuance, (b) add a proxy/gateway layer that injects per-call metadata for finer attribution than key-level alone. Recommended sequence: run showback for 4-6 weeks until ~80% of spend is attributed, then flip to chargeback.
providers: generic; third-party gateway tools (LiteLLM, Portkey, Helicone) cited by secondary sources, not independently verified
savings: Not a direct $ saving — an enabling control that FinOps Foundation frames as the prerequisite for both showback and chargeback.
effort: Medium: real engineering work despite being organizationally framed as 'non-technical'
trap: A metadata-only proxy (headers/logging) stays tier A; but some gateway products also do routing/caching/rewriting of the actual request, which crosses into tier B/C territory — verify exactly what the gateway does to the request, not just what it claims to do.
